notes: Explaining the meaning of History and the meaning of past events.
General Competence: Communication
General Competence: Analytical Thinking
Specific Competence 1.1.1.1: Communicate relevance of past events.

Show the class two picture cards: (a) an old black-and-white photograph of Mkushi Boma taken in the 1960s; (b) a recent photograph of Mkushi town today. Ask: "What is the difference between picture A and picture B? What happened between the time picture A was taken and today?" State the lesson goal: "Today we define History and define past events."

1. Define History: Explain History as a scientific study of man, his accomplishments and failures, and the evolution of human society in political, social, economic, artistic, religious and other terms. Write the definition on the chalkboard. 2. Define Past Events: Explain a past event as anything that happened before the present moment, ranging from a family funeral or wedding held last year, to national events such as Zambia's independence in 1964, to global events such as the First World War. 3. Key Words: Guide learners to identify key words in each definition (scientific study, accomplishments, failures, evolution, before the present). 4. Group Activity: Put learners in groups of five. Give each group manila paper. Ask them to list 3 examples of past events from their own family or village in Central Province, e.g. a wedding at a school hall, a funeral in Fiwila village, or the opening of a boarding STEM school. 5. Real-Life Applications: History as a subject at their school; the history of the Bemba, Tonga and Lozi people of Zambia; the history of the Zambia National Football Team's 1994 Gabon air disaster and its aftermath. 6. Synthesis: Summarise the definitions of History and past events on the chalkboard, using Fig 1.1.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. Define History. 2. Define a past event, giving one example from your own life. 3. Chanda, a Form 1 pupil, says History is only about things that happened 'a very long time ago' and that yesterday's events cannot be part of History. Using your definition, explain to Chanda TWO reasons why this statement is not entirely correct. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: You are a Form 1 pupil at the school. Your young cousin Mutale, who has just started Grade 5 at Mkushi Primary School, tells you she does not understand why she must learn about 'things that already happened' when she could instead learn about 'things happening now'. Task 1: Explain to Mutale the meaning of History. (5 marks) Task 2: Explain to Mutale the meaning of a past event, using an example from your own family. (5 marks) Task 3: Analyse why it is still useful to study things that already happened even though they cannot be changed. (10 marks)

Assign: "Interview one family member or neighbour in your community (e.g. Mkushi Boma or your home village). Ask them to describe one past event they remember clearly. Write a short paragraph stating what the event was and when it happened."

1. Recap: "History is a scientific study of man's accomplishments, failures and the evolution of society; a past event is anything that happened before the present moment." 2. Preview: "Next, we will describe specific types of past events, such as family funerals, weddings and outings."
Describing past events, e.g. family funerals, weddings, outings.
General Competence: Citizenship

Ask learners: "Who among you attended a wedding, a funeral, or a family outing in the last year?" Ask two or three volunteers to briefly share what they attended. Write the three categories on the chalkboard: Funerals, Weddings, Outings. State the lesson goal: "Today we describe different types of past events from our families and communities."

1. Funerals: Explain that funerals are past events that mark the passing of a family or community member, e.g. the funeral of a Senior Chief in Central Province, attended by relatives from Mkushi, Serenje and Kapiri Mposhi. 2. Weddings: Explain that weddings are past events celebrating marriage, often combining Christian, Islamic or traditional customs, e.g. a wedding held at Mkushi United Church of Zambia followed by a traditional 'kitchen party'. 3. Outings: Explain that outings are past events such as school trips, church picnics, or family visits, e.g. a Form 1 educational tour to the Nachikufu Caves in Mpika District, or a family outing to Kundalila Falls in Serenje. 4. Group Activity: In groups of five, learners use the three-column manila paper to list one real example of a funeral, a wedding and an outing from their own experience. 5. Real-Life Application: Compare a rural funeral ceremony in a village near Mkushi with an urban funeral in Kabwe, noting similarities (mourning, gathering of relatives) and differences (scale, use of funeral homes). 6. Synthesis: Summarise the three categories on the chalkboard and introduce the personal timeline (Fig 1.2) as a way of recording such events in order.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. Give ONE example of a past event that is a funeral. 2. Give ONE example of a past event that is a wedding. 3. Mwansa says outings such as school trips are 'not important enough' to be called past events, and that only funerals and weddings count. Using your notes, explain to Mwansa TWO reasons why his statement is incorrect. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: Your class at the school is preparing a 'Family History Day' where each learner presents one past event from their family. Your friend Natasha says she has 'nothing to present' because her family has never had a wedding or funeral recently. Task 1: Identify TWO other categories of past events Natasha could describe besides funerals and weddings. (4 marks) Task 2: Describe how Natasha could present a family outing as a past event for the Family History Day. (6 marks) Task 3: Explain why it is important for every family, however small its recent history, to have something worth recording for such an event. (10 marks)
Assign: "Draw your own simple timeline (like Fig 1.2) showing FOUR past events from your own life, in the correct order, with approximate dates."

1. Recap: "Past events can be described under categories such as funerals, weddings and outings, each with real Zambian examples from our own lives." 2. Preview: "Next, we will describe the importance of past events, focusing on how they help provide solutions to present and future problems."
Describing the importance of past events: past experiences can provide present or future solutions (Part A).
General Competence: Critical Thinking
General Competence: Problem Solving

Read a short account: "In 2024, Zambia experienced a severe drought. Government used lessons from the 1991-92 drought to plan measures such as increased Farmer Input Support and Cash-for-Work programmes." Ask: "How did knowledge of a past drought help leaders respond better to a new drought?" State the lesson goal: "Today we explain how past experiences provide solutions to present and future problems."

1. Explain that past experiences record what worked and what failed, giving present and future leaders and citizens evidence to make better decisions. 2. Example 1 (Agriculture): The 1991-92 drought taught Zambia to diversify crops and build the Food Reserve Agency's grain reserves, informing the government's 2024 drought response measures. 3. Example 2 (Health): Lessons from the cholera outbreaks in Lusaka's compounds in past decades inform present-day sanitation and vaccination campaigns in urban areas such as Kanyama and Chawama. 4. Example 3 (Personal): A learner who once failed an examination after not revising can use that past experience to plan better study habits for present and future examinations. 5. Group Activity: In groups, learners identify one problem in their own community (e.g. flooding along the Mkushi River, road accidents on the Great North Road) and suggest how looking at past occurrences of the same problem could help solve it today. 6. Synthesis: Summarise on the chalkboard using Fig 1.3, showing 'solving present/future problems' as one key reason for studying past events.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. Explain ONE way in which past experiences can provide solutions to present problems. 2. Give ONE Zambian example of a past event being used to solve a present problem. 3. Kondwani argues that since 'the past is gone and cannot be changed', it is a waste of time to study it when solving today's problems. Using ONE example, explain to Kondwani why his statement is incorrect. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: You are a member of the Environmental Club at the school. Central Province has experienced repeated flooding along the Mkushi River during the rainy season for the past three years, damaging roads and fields. The Club has been asked to advise the Parent-Teacher Association on how historical knowledge of past floods could help solve the current problem. Task 1: Explain how studying records of past floods in the area can help the community understand the current flooding problem. (6 marks) Task 2: Suggest TWO practical solutions the community could adopt based on lessons from the past. (8 marks) Task 3: Explain why some communities fail to learn from history and continue repeating the same mistakes. (6 marks)
Assign: "Write a paragraph describing one problem your family or community faced before, and explain how remembering that past experience could help solve a similar problem if it happened again."

1. Recap: "Past experiences provide evidence that helps solve present and future problems, as seen in agriculture, health and personal examples." 2. Preview: "Next, we continue looking at the importance of past events, focusing on becoming better citizens and developing critical thinking."
Describing the importance of past events: becoming better citizens and developing critical thinking (Part B).

Show the Zambian flag or a picture of it. Ask: "What past event does our national flag remind us of?" Guide learners to recall Zambia's independence on 24th October 1964. State the lesson goal: "Today we explain how past events help us become better citizens and develop critical thinking."

1. Citizenship: Explain that knowing our history helps us appreciate our national identity, respect the sacrifices of past leaders such as Dr Kenneth Kaunda, and participate meaningfully in national events like Independence Day and Youth Day celebrated at Mkushi Boma. 2. Critical Thinking: Explain that studying past events trains learners to question sources, compare different accounts, and reach reasoned conclusions rather than accepting information blindly, e.g. comparing two elders' differing accounts of when a village was founded near Mkushi. 3. Example: A Form 1 pupil who studies the history of the Zambian independence struggle is more likely to value voting, respect the Constitution, and participate in community development such as Constituency Development Fund (CDF) projects. 4. Group Activity: In groups, learners discuss one national value (e.g. 'One Zambia, One Nation') and explain how knowledge of history strengthens that value. 5. Real-Life Application: Comparing how different regions of Zambia (e.g. Central, Copperbelt and Western Provinces) contributed differently to the independence struggle, and how this diversity is now a source of national pride rather than division. 6. Synthesis: Complete Fig 1.3, now showing all four reasons for studying past events (problem-solving, citizenship, critical thinking, avoiding repeated mistakes).

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. State ONE way in which studying past events helps a person become a better citizen. 2. State ONE way in which studying past events develops critical thinking. 3. Bwalya says that only politicians need to know history to be 'good citizens', and that ordinary pupils do not need it. Explain to Bwalya TWO reasons why his statement is incorrect. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: Every year, the school holds an Independence Day celebration on 24th October. This year, the Head Teacher has asked the History Club to lead a short presentation to remind pupils why the celebration matters. Some pupils have complained that the celebration is 'just a holiday for resting' and has no real value. Task 1: Explain how understanding the history of Zambia's independence struggle can make pupils better citizens. (6 marks) Task 2: Explain how studying such history can help pupils develop critical thinking when they hear different opinions about national issues. (6 marks) Task 3: Suggest TWO activities the History Club could include in the presentation to make the celebration more meaningful to pupils. (8 marks)
Assign: "Write a short paragraph explaining, in your own words, why you personally think it is important to be a well-informed citizen who knows the history of Zambia."

1. Recap: "Studying past events helps people become better citizens by building national identity and civic responsibility, and develops critical thinking by training learners to question and compare sources." 2. Preview: "Next, we will show the importance of history in different fields, beginning with Medicine."
Showing the importance of history in different fields/topics: Medicine.

Ask: "Has anyone here ever had malaria? How is malaria treated today compared to how it might have been treated fifty years ago?" Allow two or three learners to share what they know. State the lesson goal: "Today we show the importance of history in the field of Medicine."

1. Explain that History helps in Medicine by understanding the origin of diseases and treatment, e.g. tracing how malaria has affected communities in Mkushi District over decades and how prevention methods (mosquito nets, indoor spraying) have evolved. 2. Explain that History helps in understanding patterns and trends in disease progression, e.g. studying past cholera outbreak records in Lusaka to predict and prevent future outbreaks in urban compounds. 3. Give a further example: the history of HIV/AIDS in Zambia, from its emergence in the 1980s to the present-day Antiretroviral Therapy (ART) programmes at Mkushi District Hospital, shows how historical understanding of a disease informs present treatment and public health policy. 4. Group Activity: In groups, learners discuss one disease common in their community (e.g. malaria, cholera, diarrhoea) and suggest how knowing its history in the area could help health workers respond better today. 5. Real-Life Application: Compare traditional herbal treatments once used in villages near Mkushi with the antimalarial medicines used at Mkushi District Hospital today, showing how historical knowledge of both informs a fuller understanding of health practices. 6. Synthesis: Summarise on the chalkboard using Fig 1.4, highlighting the Medicine link.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. State ONE way History is useful in Medicine. 2. Give ONE Zambian example showing the link between History and Medicine. 3. Chileshe argues that doctors 'only need science, not history' to treat patients. Explain to Chileshe TWO reasons why understanding history is also useful to doctors. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: Mkushi District Hospital has recorded a sharp rise in malaria cases this rainy season, similar to an outbreak that occurred five years ago. The District Health Office has asked the History Club at the school to help create awareness materials linking the past outbreak to the present situation. Task 1: Explain how studying the history of the malaria outbreak five years ago can help health workers respond to the current outbreak. (6 marks) Task 2: Suggest TWO pieces of information from the past outbreak that would be most useful to include in the awareness materials. (8 marks) Task 3: Explain why some communities continue to suffer repeated disease outbreaks despite having experienced them before. (6 marks)

Assign: "Research (by asking a parent, guardian, or clinic worker, or using any available source) one disease that has affected your community in the past and is still a concern today. Write two sentences on how its history could help prevent it in future."

1. Recap: "History is important in Medicine because it helps us understand the origins, patterns and trends of diseases, guiding present and future treatment." 2. Preview: "Next, we will show the importance of history in the field of Music."
Showing the importance of history in different fields/topics: Music.
General Competence: Creativity and Innovation

Ask learners to name a Zambian musician, past or present, whose music they enjoy (e.g. Alick Nkhata, PK Chishala, or a contemporary artist). Ask: "Why do we still remember and enjoy some old Zambian songs today?" State the lesson goal: "Today we show the importance of history in the field of Music."

1. Explain that History helps in Music by identifying influential composers and musicians, e.g. remembering pioneers of Zambian music such as Alick Nkhata, whose songs shaped early Zambian national identity. 2. Explain that History helps in appreciating cultural and social contexts of music, e.g. understanding why Kalindula music became popular during the 1970s and how it reflected Zambian social life at the time. 3. Explain that History helps musicians and listeners learn from past music masters and innovators, e.g. how present-day Zambian artists blend traditional Bemba, Tonga or Lozi rhythms with modern genres, building on musical traditions passed down over generations. 4. Group Activity: In groups, learners list one traditional song or dance from their own area (e.g. Vinkhanyakha songs of the Bisa people near Mkushi, or songs sung at the Nc'wala ceremony) and discuss what it tells us about the history of that community. 5. Real-Life Application: Compare how traditional ceremonial songs performed at events like the Kulamba ceremony of the Chewa preserve historical memory of a chiefdom's origins and migrations. 6. Synthesis: Complete Fig 1.4 by adding notes under the Music branch.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. State ONE way History is useful in Music. 2. Give ONE Zambian example showing the link between History and Music. 3. Given argues that music is 'just for entertainment' and has nothing to do with history. Explain to Given TWO reasons why his statement is incorrect. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: The Cultural Club at the school has been invited to perform at the district's annual cultural gala, where different schools showcase traditional songs and dances from their local communities in Central Province. Some pupils feel that learning 'old traditional songs' is a waste of time compared to learning modern music. Task 1: Explain the importance of learning the history behind traditional songs and dances before performing them. (6 marks) Task 2: Explain how traditional music can help preserve a community's history for future generations. (6 marks) Task 3: Suggest ONE way the Cultural Club could combine traditional and modern music to make their performance both historically meaningful and appealing to a young audience. (8 marks)

Assign: "Ask an elder in your family or community to teach you the words or story behind one traditional song from your home area. Write down what the song is about and what it tells us about the community's history."

1. Recap: "History is important in Music because it helps us identify influential musicians, understand cultural contexts, and learn from past musical traditions." 2. Preview: "Next, we will show the importance of history in the field of Law."
Showing the importance of history in different fields/topics: Law.

Ask: "If a court in Mkushi is deciding a new case, should the judge look at how similar cases were decided in the past?" Allow learners to give their opinions. State the lesson goal: "Today we show the importance of history in the field of Law."

1. Explain that History helps in Law by making reference to similar past cases to make judgments on present cases, a principle known as legal precedent. 2. Explain with an example: Zambian courts, including the Constitutional Court, often refer to earlier rulings on similar matters (e.g. past election petition cases) when deciding a new case, ensuring consistency and fairness. 3. Explain that History also helps lawmakers understand why certain laws were created, e.g. understanding the history of traditional land tenure in Central Province helps legislators draft fair modern land laws that respect customary rights around Mkushi. 4. Group Activity/Role Play: Divide learners into small groups. Give each group a simple mock scenario (e.g. a dispute over a borrowed bicycle in Mkushi) and ask them to imagine they are a traditional court, using a similar 'past case' example provided to help decide the present one. 5. Real-Life Application: Discuss how Zambia's Constitution has been amended several times (e.g. in 1991, 1996, and 2016), each amendment drawing on the historical experience of how earlier constitutional provisions worked or failed. 6. Synthesis: Complete Fig 1.4 fully, summarising the Medicine, Music and Law examples together.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. State ONE way History is useful in Law. 2. Give ONE Zambian example showing the link between History and Law. 3. Natasha argues that 'every case is different', so looking at the past is useless in law. Explain to Natasha TWO reasons why her statement is incorrect. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: A land dispute has arisen between two families near Mkushi over a piece of farmland that has been used by both families' ancestors for generations. The local traditional court is considering how to decide the case fairly. Task 1: Explain how knowledge of the land's history could help the traditional court resolve this dispute fairly. (6 marks) Task 2: Explain how referring to similar past land cases could guide the court's decision. (6 marks) Task 3: Suggest TWO sources of historical information the court could use to establish the true history of the land. (8 marks)

Assign: "Ask a parent, guardian or community elder to explain one traditional rule or law in your area (e.g. about land, marriage, or borrowing property) and how it has been applied in the past to solve a dispute. Write a short paragraph summarising what you learnt."

1. Recap: "History is important in Law because courts and lawmakers use knowledge of past cases and past experiences to make fair present-day decisions." 2. Preview: "Next, we will move to Sub-Topic 1.1.2 and discuss local history, beginning with the history of our own township or village."
Discussing the history of your township/village.
General Competence: Communication
General Competence: Citizenship
Specific Competence 1.1.2.1: Interpret local history.

Ask learners: "Who can tell me one old building or landmark in Mkushi Boma or your home village that has 'always been there' since before you were born?" Allow two or three responses. State the lesson goal: "Today we discuss the history of our own township or village."

1. Explain that every township or village has its own history, including when and how it was established, who its early settlers were, and important events that shaped it. 2. Use Mkushi Boma as a working example: discuss its establishment as a district administrative centre, its growth along the Great North Road, and landmarks such as the Boma offices, a local boarding STEM school, and the local market. 3. Explain that township/village history also includes the story of the local Chieftainship (e.g. the Senior Chief presiding over the area) and how the community related to neighbouring villages and districts such as Serenje and Kapiri Mposhi. 4. Group Activity: In groups, learners discuss and note down what they know or can find out about the establishment of their own home village or township (name, approximate date/period of settlement, founder/first settlers if known). 5. Real-Life Application: Compare the history of Mkushi Boma with that of a nearby town such as Kapiri Mposhi, noting similarities (both grew along transport routes) and differences (different founding dates and economic activities). 6. Synthesis: Summarise using Fig 1.5, showing key landmarks and their historical significance in Mkushi Boma.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. State ONE fact about the history of Mkushi Boma. 2. Name ONE landmark in your own township or village and explain its historical significance. 3. Chola says his village 'has no history' because it is small and not well known. Explain to Chola TWO reasons why his statement is incorrect. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: The Mkushi District Council is compiling a booklet on the history of townships and villages in the district ahead of the district's 60th anniversary celebrations. Your class has been asked to contribute a short write-up on the history of your own home area. Task 1: Identify THREE types of information you would need to gather about your home area's history for the booklet. (6 marks) Task 2: Explain how you would gather this information, mentioning at least two different sources. (8 marks) Task 3: Explain why it is important for a district council to preserve and publish the history of its townships and villages. (6 marks)
Assign: "Ask a parent, guardian or elder in your community: 'When and how was our village/township first settled?' Write down what you learn in a short paragraph."

1. Recap: "Every township or village, however small, has its own history of settlement, leadership and development, as illustrated by Mkushi Boma." 2. Preview: "Next, we will analyse the developments that have taken place in our township or village in the recent past."
Analysing the developments that have taken place in your township/village in the recent past.
General Competence: Analytical Thinking
General Competence: Environmental Sustainability

Ask: "What is one new building, road, or service that has appeared in Mkushi or your home area within your own lifetime?" Allow two or three responses. State the lesson goal: "Today we analyse developments that have taken place in our township or village in the recent past."

1. Explain that 'recent past' developments refer to changes that have occurred within roughly the last two to three decades, which many living residents can remember or verify. 2. Use Mkushi Boma as a working example: discuss developments such as the extension of the electricity grid, tarring of roads, growth of the market, and expansion of schools and clinics. 3. Explain the skill of analysis: not just listing developments, but explaining their causes (e.g. government investment, population growth) and their effects (e.g. improved living standards, increased trade). 4. Group Activity: In groups, learners construct a simple timeline (similar to Fig 1.6) of three to five recent developments in their own home area, noting approximate dates and effects. 5. Real-Life Application: Discuss how the tarring of the Mkushi-Serenje road affected trade and travel time between the two towns, linking cause (infrastructure investment) to effect (economic growth). 6. Synthesis: Summarise using Fig 1.6, and emphasise that analysing development also requires considering both positive and negative effects, e.g. new roads bringing both economic growth and increased traffic accidents.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. State ONE recent development that has taken place in Mkushi Boma or your own home area. 2. Give ONE effect of a recent development you identified. 3. Mutinta says that 'nothing important has changed' in her village in the recent past. Explain to Mutinta TWO reasons why she might be wrong, and how she could check. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: The school is preparing a display for Open Day showing 'How Our District Has Changed' over the past 20 years, using information gathered by pupils from their own home areas. Task 1: Identify THREE categories of development your group could investigate for the display (e.g. infrastructure, education, health). (6 marks) Task 2: Explain how you would gather accurate information on developments in each category. (8 marks) Task 3: Analyse ONE possible negative effect that can come with rapid local development, and suggest how the community could manage it. (6 marks)
Assign: "Draw a simple timeline (like Fig 1.6) of THREE developments that have taken place in your own home area in the recent past, with approximate dates and one effect for each."

1. Recap: "Analysing recent developments in our township/village involves identifying changes, their causes and their effects, both positive and negative." 2. Preview: "Next, we will examine the importance of local history more broadly."
Examining the importance of local history.
General Competence: Entrepreneurship

Ask: "Why do you think Mkushi District Council keeps records of its own history, instead of only relying on national history books?" Allow two or three responses. State the lesson goal: "Today we examine the importance of local history to a community."

1. Explain that local history builds a sense of identity and belonging, helping residents of Mkushi District understand their roots and feel proud of their community. 2. Explain that local history preserves cultural heritage, such as traditions, ceremonies and landmarks specific to the area, for future generations. 3. Explain that local history can support entrepreneurship and tourism, e.g. heritage sites near Mkushi District attracting visitors, creating opportunities for guiding, crafts and hospitality businesses. 4. Group Activity: In groups, learners rank three reasons why local history is important (identity, heritage preservation, economic/tourism opportunity) in order of importance to their own community, and justify their ranking. 5. Real-Life Application: Discuss how documenting the history of a local chiefdom or heritage feature could be developed into a small tourism/education initiative benefiting the local community economically. 6. Synthesis: Adapt Fig 1.3 to summarise the importance of local history under identity, heritage preservation, and economic opportunity.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. State ONE reason why local history is important to a community. 2. State ONE way local history can create economic opportunities for a community. 3. Chanda argues that only national history (like Zambia's independence) matters, and that local history 'is not important enough' to study. Explain to Chanda TWO reasons why his statement is incorrect. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: A group of young people in Mkushi District has identified an old, little-known historical site near their village that was once an early settlement, but it currently attracts no visitors and is not well documented. The Mkushi District Youth Development Committee wants to know if the site can be turned into a community project. Task 1: Explain the importance of documenting the history of this site before developing it. (6 marks) Task 2: Suggest TWO ways the youths could turn the site into a source of income for the community. (8 marks) Task 3: Explain ONE challenge the youths might face in preserving and promoting the site, and how they could overcome it. (6 marks)
Assign: "Write a paragraph proposing one way your own home community could benefit (socially or economically) from documenting and promoting its local history."

1. Recap: "Local history is important because it builds identity and belonging, preserves cultural heritage, and can create entrepreneurship and tourism opportunities." 2. Preview: "Next, we move to Sub-Topic 1.1.3 and begin classifying the types or branches of History."
Identifying types/branches of history study: the Chronological branch (Ancient, Medieval, Modern history).
General Competence: Analytical Thinking
General Competence: Digital Literacy
Specific Competence 1.1.3.1: Classify types or branches of history.

Draw a long line on the chalkboard representing time, from 'earliest times' to 'today'. Ask: "If we divide all of human history into three big blocks of time, what might we call the earliest, the middle, and the most recent block?" State the lesson goal: "Today we identify the chronological branches of History: Ancient, Medieval and Modern."

1. Explain that History can be classified chronologically, that is, according to time periods. 2. Ancient History: covers the earliest human societies up to around the 5th century, e.g. the Stone Age communities that lived in present-day Zambia, evidence of which is found at sites such as Kalambo Falls. 3. Medieval History: covers roughly the 5th to 15th centuries, including the growth of early Bantu-speaking communities and Iron Age farming settlements in Zambia, such as those at Kalundu near Kalomo. 4. Modern History: covers the 15th century to the present, including the arrival of European explorers and missionaries, colonial rule, and Zambia's independence in 1964 up to present-day events. 5. Group Activity: In groups, learners sort a list of given events (e.g. 'Stone Age tools used in Zambia', 'Zambia gains independence', 'Early Iron Age farming communities settle in Zambia') into the correct chronological branch. 6. Synthesis: Summarise using Fig 1.7, showing the three chronological branches in order.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. Name the THREE chronological branches of History. 2. Give ONE Zambian example that would fall under Ancient History. 3. Mwape says that 'History is History' and that dividing it into Ancient, Medieval and Modern is unnecessary. Explain to Mwape TWO reasons why this classification is useful. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: The History Club at the school is preparing a timeline wall-chart for the classroom, showing key events from Zambia's past arranged chronologically. A new Form 1 pupil, Chomba, is confused about where to place events such as 'the introduction of Iron Age farming' and 'Zambia's independence' on the chart. Task 1: Explain to Chomba the meaning of the three chronological branches of History. (6 marks) Task 2: Correctly classify 'the introduction of Iron Age farming in Zambia' and 'Zambia's independence in 1964' into their correct chronological branches, giving reasons. (8 marks) Task 3: Explain why a wall-chart timeline is a useful learning tool for a History classroom. (6 marks)
Assign: "Draw a simple timeline dividing it into Ancient, Medieval and Modern History, and place TWO events from your notes correctly under each branch."

1. Recap: "History can be classified chronologically into Ancient, Medieval and Modern branches, each covering a different broad time period." 2. Preview: "Next, we will identify the thematic and geographical branches of History, such as Political, Social, Economic, World and African History."
Identifying types/branches of history study: Thematic branches (Political, Social, Economic) and Geographical branches (World History, African History, Music History, Sport History).
General Competence: Collaboration

Ask: "If you wanted to study only how Zambia's leaders and government have changed over time, which 'branch' of history would that be? What if you wanted to study only how people's daily lives and traditions have changed?" Allow learners to suggest possible names. State the lesson goal: "Today we identify the thematic and geographical branches of History."

1. Explain Political History: the study of governments, leaders and power, e.g. the history of Zambia's presidents from Dr Kenneth Kaunda to the present. 2. Explain Social History: the study of everyday life, traditions and society, e.g. the history of traditional ceremonies such as the Nc'wala ceremony of the Ngoni. 3. Explain Economic History: the study of trade, industry and money, e.g. the history of copper mining on the Copperbelt and its impact on Zambia's economy. 4. Explain Geographical branches: World History (covering global events, e.g. the World Wars) and African History (covering events across the African continent, e.g. the Scramble for Africa); also mention Music History and Sport History as specialised branches. 5. Group Activity: In groups, learners match five given topics (e.g. 'the history of Zambia's copper mines', 'the history of the Nc'wala ceremony', 'the history of Chipolopolo football team', 'the history of Zambia's presidents', 'the history of the First World War') to the correct branch of History. 6. Synthesis: Summarise using Fig 1.8, showing all thematic and geographical branches together.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. Name TWO thematic branches of History. 2. Give ONE example of a topic that falls under Economic History in Zambia. 3. Chibwe says that Sport History and Music History are 'not real history' because they are not about politics or war. Explain to Chibwe TWO reasons why his statement is incorrect. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: The History Club at the school is organising a 'Branches of History' exhibition, where each group presents a poster on a different branch of History using local or national Zambian examples. Task 1: Identify FOUR different branches of History that different groups could each choose to present (from either the thematic or geographical branches). (8 marks) Task 2: Choose ONE branch and describe, with a Zambian example, what that branch of History studies. (6 marks) Task 3: Explain why studying History through different branches, rather than as one single subject, is useful for learners. (6 marks)
Assign: "Choose any THREE branches of History discussed today and, for each, write one Zambian topic that would fall under that branch."

1. Recap: "History has thematic branches (Political, Social, Economic) and geographical/specialised branches (World, African, Music, Sport History), each focusing on a different aspect or area of study." 2. Preview: "Next, we will practise classifying branches of History through a hands-on sorting activity."
Classifying branches of history (hands-on practical sorting activity).
General Competence: Problem Solving

Quickly review the branches of History covered in Lessons 11 and 12 by asking learners to name as many as they can remember in 60 seconds. Explain that today's lesson is a hands-on classification game. State the lesson goal: "Today we practise classifying different topics into their correct branches of History."

1. Distribute small topic cards to groups, e.g. 'Stone Age tools in Zambia', 'the presidency of Dr Kenneth Kaunda', 'the Nc'wala ceremony', 'copper mining history', 'the Second World War', 'the history of the African continent's colonisation', 'the history of Zambian musician Alick Nkhata', 'the history of the Zambia national football team'. 2. Explain the sorting chart (Fig 1.9), with columns for Chronological (Ancient/Medieval/Modern), Thematic (Political/Social/Economic), and Geographical (World/African) branches, and rows for Music and Sport History as specialised branches. 3. Guide learners through one worked example, e.g. placing 'the presidency of Dr Kenneth Kaunda' under Political History (thematic) and also under Modern History (chronological), showing that one topic can belong to more than one branch. 4. Group Activity: Learners sort all their topic cards onto the manila paper sorting chart, discussing and justifying their placements within the group. 5. Class Review: Groups present their sorting chart; the class discusses and corrects any misclassifications together. 6. Synthesis: Summarise the key lesson that classification is a tool for organising knowledge, and that some topics fit more than one branch.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. Classify the topic 'the history of copper mining on the Copperbelt' into its correct thematic branch of History. 2. Classify the topic 'the Nc'wala ceremony of the Ngoni people' into its correct thematic branch of History. 3. Namutowe struggles to classify the topic 'Zambia's independence in 1964', saying it could fit under more than one branch. Explain to Namutowe why a single historical topic can sometimes belong to more than one branch of History, using this example. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: Your History teacher has organised a classification competition between groups at the school. Each group is given a set of topic cards and must correctly classify each one within a time limit, explaining their reasoning to earn full marks. Your group receives the cards: 'Stone Age tools found in Zambia', 'the history of Chipolopolo (Zambia's football team)', and 'the Second World War'. Task 1: Classify each of the THREE given topics into its correct branch(es) of History. (9 marks) Task 2: Explain the reasoning behind your classification for ONE of the three topics. (6 marks) Task 3: Explain ONE benefit of being able to correctly classify historical topics into their branches. (5 marks)
Assign: "Choose any FIVE topics from your own knowledge (Zambian or global) and classify each one into its correct branch(es) of History, giving a one-sentence reason for each."

1. Recap: "Classifying History into chronological, thematic and geographical branches helps organise knowledge, and some topics belong to more than one branch at once." 2. Preview: "Next, we move to Sub-Topic 1.1.4 and begin discussing the sources of History, starting with oral tradition and written records."
Discussing methods of gathering information about the past: Oral tradition and Written records.
General Competence: Analytical Thinking
General Competence: Communication
Specific Competence 1.1.4.1: Assess credibility of sources of historical information.

Ask: "If historians want to know what happened in a Zambian village 100 years ago, but there is no book about it, how could they find out?" Allow learners to suggest ideas (e.g. asking elders, looking for old documents). State the lesson goal: "Today we discuss oral tradition and written records as methods of gathering historical information."

1. Explain Oral Tradition: information passed down by word of mouth through stories, songs, praise poems and proverbs, e.g. Bemba, Tonga, Lozi and other Zambian communities preserving their chiefdom histories through oral tradition passed from elders to youths. 2. Explain Written Records: information recorded in books, letters, newspapers, missionary diaries and government files, e.g. missionary records from stations such as Mbereshi and Chilubula documenting early colonial-era Zambia. 3. Show the sample old letter/newspaper cutting/church record and discuss what kind of historical information it could reveal. 4. Group Activity: In groups, learners list two questions they could ask a village elder to gather oral tradition about their community's past, and two types of written records they could search for at a local council, church or school office. 5. Real-Life Application: Discuss how National Archives of Zambia in Lusaka preserves written colonial-era records, while village elders in areas like Mkushi remain living sources of oral tradition. 6. Synthesis: Summarise using Fig 1.10, contrasting oral tradition and written records.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. Define oral tradition as a source of history. 2. Give ONE example of a written record that can be used as a source of history. 3. Bupe says that only written records are 'proper' history, and that oral tradition should not be trusted at all. Explain to Bupe TWO reasons why her statement is too extreme. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: A group of Form 1 pupils at the school has been asked to research the history of a local Chieftainship in Central Province for a class project, but the school library has very few written books on the topic. Task 1: Explain how the pupils could use oral tradition to gather information for their project. (6 marks) Task 2: Suggest TWO possible written sources the pupils could still search for, even with a limited school library. (6 marks) Task 3: Explain ONE challenge the pupils might face when relying mainly on oral tradition, and how they could address it. (8 marks)
Assign: "Interview one elder in your family or community using at least two questions about the history of your area, and write down what they told you, noting that this is oral tradition."

1. Recap: "Oral tradition and written records are two important methods of gathering information about the past, each with its own strengths." 2. Preview: "Next, we will discuss further methods of gathering historical information: anthropology, archaeology, linguistics and genetics."
Discussing methods of gathering information about the past: Anthropology, Archaeology, Linguistics and Genetics.
General Competence: Digital Literacy

Ask: "If archaeologists dig up an old clay pot near Kalambo Falls, what could that single pot tell us about the people who lived there long ago?" Allow learners to speculate (e.g. what they ate, their skills, their trade). State the lesson goal: "Today we discuss archaeology and other scientific methods of gathering historical information."

1. Explain Archaeology: the scientific study of past human life through excavation of artefacts such as tools, pottery and remains, e.g. archaeological finds at Kalambo Falls and Nachikufu Caves revealing Zambia's Stone Age past. 2. Explain Anthropology: the study of human culture, society and customs, e.g. anthropologists studying the traditional customs and social organisation of the Bemba or Lozi people to understand their historical way of life. 3. Explain Linguistics: the study of how languages develop and change over time, e.g. linguists tracing the spread of Bantu languages across Africa, including into present-day Zambia, to understand ancient migration patterns. 4. Explain Genetics: the study of DNA to trace human ancestry and migration, e.g. genetic studies helping confirm the routes taken by early Bantu-speaking migrants into Zambia from Central and West Africa. 5. Group Activity: In groups, learners match four scenarios (e.g. 'digging up old pottery', 'comparing traditional customs of two communities', 'studying how a language changed over 500 years', 'using DNA to trace ancestry') to the correct scientific method. 6. Synthesis: Summarise using Fig 1.11, showing all four scientific sources together.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. Define archaeology as a source of historical information. 2. Give ONE example of how genetics can be used to study history. 3. Kabwe says that scientific methods like archaeology and genetics are 'too complicated' to be useful for ordinary History lessons. Explain to Kabwe TWO reasons why these methods are still important to understand. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: A team of archaeologists has discovered ancient stone tools and pottery fragments at a new site near Mkushi District, believed to be evidence of an early Stone Age community. The National Heritage Conservation Commission has asked local schools, including the school, to help raise awareness about the discovery. Task 1: Explain how archaeology helped uncover evidence of this early community. (6 marks) Task 2: Suggest how anthropology and linguistics could be used alongside archaeology to build a fuller picture of the community's history. (8 marks) Task 3: Explain why it is important to protect such archaeological sites from disturbance by the public. (6 marks)

Assign: "Choose ONE of the four scientific methods discussed today (archaeology, anthropology, linguistics or genetics) and write a short paragraph explaining, in your own words, how it helps historians learn about the past."

1. Recap: "Archaeology, anthropology, linguistics and genetics are scientific methods that provide physical and biological evidence about the past, complementing oral tradition and written records." 2. Preview: "Next, we will analyse the reliability of these different methods of gathering information about the past."
Analysing the reliability of methods of gathering information about the past.
General Competence: Critical Thinking

Read out two short, deliberately conflicting accounts of an imaginary event (e.g. two different descriptions of 'what happened at Mkushi market last Saturday'). Ask: "Both accounts cannot be completely true. How would you decide which one to trust, or how much of each to trust?" State the lesson goal: "Today we analyse the reliability of different sources of historical information."

1. Explain that reliability means how trustworthy and accurate a source is, and that no single source is automatically 100% reliable or unreliable. 2. Explain factors that affect reliability: closeness to the event in time and place (eyewitness vs second-hand), the bias or motive of the source, whether the account can be cross-checked against other sources, and how well-preserved physical evidence is. 3. Example: a single elder's oral account of a chiefdom's founding may be less reliable alone, but becomes more reliable when it matches accounts from several other elders and is supported by archaeological findings in the same area. 4. Group Activity: In groups, learners rank five given sources (e.g. 'a rumour heard from a friend', 'a single oral account from one elder', 'a government land record', 'a newspaper article from the time of the event', 'archaeological evidence cross-checked with written records') from least to most reliable, giving reasons. 5. Real-Life Application: Discuss how historians studying Zambia's pre-colonial chiefdoms cross-check oral traditions collected from different villages against archaeological finds and early written traveller accounts to build the most reliable picture possible. 6. Synthesis: Summarise using Fig 1.12, the reliability scale.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. State ONE factor that affects the reliability of a historical source. 2. Between a single, unverified rumour and a government record cross-checked with other evidence, which is generally more reliable, and why? 3. Kalaba says that written records are 'always' more reliable than oral tradition, with no exceptions. Explain to Kalaba TWO reasons why this is not always true. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: Two elders in a village near Mkushi give different accounts of when their village was first settled: one says '80 years ago', the other says '120 years ago'. A written mission record from a nearby church, dated to around 100 years ago, briefly mentions 'a small settlement already existing' in the area. Task 1: Analyse the reliability of each of the two oral accounts, using the information given. (8 marks) Task 2: Explain how the written mission record could help resolve the disagreement between the two elders. (6 marks) Task 3: Suggest ONE additional method the researcher could use to further confirm the true settlement date. (6 marks)
Assign: "Choose any historical claim you have heard from a family member or in the community. Write down the claim and explain what you would need to check to find out how reliable it is."

1. Recap: "The reliability of a historical source depends on factors such as closeness to the event, possible bias, and whether it can be cross-checked with other sources." 2. Preview: "Next, we will discuss how to utilise reliable methods to write history accurately."
Utilising reliable methods to write history.

Ask: "If you were asked to write one accurate paragraph about how the school was established, what steps would you follow before writing?" Allow learners to suggest steps. State the lesson goal: "Today we practise using reliable methods to write history."

1. Explain the five steps for writing reliable history: (1) identify the topic, (2) gather information from multiple sources, (3) cross-check for accuracy, (4) arrange information in chronological order, (5) write with correct referencing of sources. 2. Model the process using the example of writing about the establishment of the school: identify the topic, gather information (interview a long-serving teacher, check school records), cross-check dates, arrange events in order, then draft a short paragraph. 3. Explain correct referencing: always stating where information came from (e.g. 'according to Mr X, a teacher who has worked at the school since...') so readers can judge the source's reliability themselves. 4. Group Activity: In groups, learners choose one local topic (e.g. the history of a nearby church, market or clinic) and plan the five steps they would follow to write a reliable short account of it. 5. Individual Practice: Learners individually draft a short paragraph (4-6 sentences) about a chosen past event from their own family or community, applying the five steps and referencing their source. 6. Synthesis: Summarise using Fig 1.13, the five-step process for writing reliable history.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. List the FIVE steps for writing reliable history. 2. Explain why referencing your source is important when writing history. 3. Chibuye wrote a paragraph about the history of his village based only on 'something he heard once', with no other checking. Explain to Chibuye TWO mistakes in his approach, based on the five steps. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: Your History teacher has assigned you to write a short, accurate account of the founding of a local market or trading centre in Mkushi District, to be included in a class booklet on local history. You have access to one elder who remembers the market's early days, and old council records mentioning the market's registration date. Task 1: Describe the steps you would follow to write a reliable account of the market's founding. (8 marks) Task 2: Explain how you would handle it if the elder's account and the council record gave slightly different dates. (6 marks) Task 3: Explain why it is important for your final written account to include references to your sources. (6 marks)
Assign: "Using the five steps learnt today, write a short, referenced paragraph (5-6 sentences) about one past event in your family's history, clearly stating your source of information."

1. Recap: "Writing reliable history involves identifying a topic, gathering and cross-checking multiple sources, arranging events chronologically, and referencing sources correctly." 2. Preview: "Next, we move to our final sub-topic, 1.1.5, and begin identifying digital resources for learning about the past."

cbc_2023__hist__g1__1_1_introduction_to_.subTopicName: 1.1.5 Learning About the Past Using Digital Resources
notes: Identifying digital resources (phone, computer, and others) for learning about the past.
General Competence: Digital Literacy
General Competence: Communication
Specific Competence 1.1.5.1: Apply digital resources in learning about the past.

Ask: "Besides asking an elder or reading a book, what electronic device could help you find information about the past today?" Allow learners to suggest devices (phone, computer, radio, television). State the lesson goal: "Today we identify digital resources that can help us learn about the past."

1. Explain that digital resources are electronic tools and platforms that can be used to access historical information. 2. Smartphones: allow internet searches, access to online encyclopaedias, and recording of oral interviews with elders (audio/video). 3. Computers/Laptops: allow access to websites, digital archives, and typed documents, useful for research projects such as those done at the school's computer laboratory. 4. Radio and Television: ZNBC and other broadcasters air documentaries and historical programmes, such as coverage of Zambia's Independence Day celebrations, which are also archived and can be a source of historical information. 5. Group Activity: In groups, learners discuss and list, for each digital resource, one advantage and one responsible-use guideline (e.g. checking that a website is trustworthy before using its information, or asking permission before recording someone). 6. Synthesis: Summarise using Fig 1.14.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. Name TWO digital resources that can be used to learn about the past. 2. State ONE way a smartphone can be used to gather historical information. 3. Musonda says that using a phone for History research is 'not serious learning' and that only books should be used. Explain to Musonda TWO reasons why digital resources are also valuable for learning history. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: The school has recently set up a small computer laboratory with limited internet access, shared between several classes. The History Club wants to use it to help pupils research the history of Zambia's National Heritage Sites. Task 1: Identify THREE digital resources or tools the History Club could use in this research, including but not limited to the computer laboratory. (6 marks) Task 2: Explain TWO responsible practices pupils should follow when using the shared computer laboratory for this research. (8 marks) Task 3: Suggest ONE way pupils without regular access to computers or smartphones could still benefit from digital resources for their history research. (6 marks)

Assign: "List THREE digital resources available in your own home or community (e.g. a family member's phone, a community radio, a cyber cafe) that you could use to research history, and state one topic you would like to research using each."

1. Recap: "Digital resources such as smartphones, computers, radio and television can all help us learn about the past, if used responsibly." 2. Preview: "Next, we will practise actually using digital resources to find new information about the past."
Using digital resources to find out new information about the past.
General Competence: Critical Thinking

Ask: "If I wanted to find out today's date in history that Zambia became a republic, and I only had a phone, what steps would I follow?" Allow learners to suggest a simple search process. State the lesson goal: "Today we practise using digital resources to find new information about the past."

1. Explain the five-step digital search process: (1) turn on the device, (2) open a browser/app, (3) type clear search terms, (4) evaluate the results for reliability, (5) record the new information found, with its source. 2. Demonstrate live (or using a prepared mock search results page) searching for a simple historical fact, e.g. 'When did Zambia become a republic?', and model how to evaluate whether a result looks reliable (checking the source, comparing more than one result). 3. Link back to Lesson 16: remind learners that not everything found online is automatically reliable, and that the same reliability factors (closeness to event, bias, cross-checking) apply to digital sources too. 4. Practical Activity: In groups (using available devices, or the mock search results page provided), learners practise the five steps to find and record one new piece of historical information about a given Zambian topic (e.g. a National Heritage Site, or a nationalist leader). 5. Real-Life Application: Discuss how museums and institutions such as the National Archives of Zambia are increasingly digitising records, making it easier for learners across the country, including at the school, to access historical information online. 6. Synthesis: Summarise using Fig 1.15.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. List the FIVE steps for using digital resources to find historical information. 2. Explain why it is important to evaluate search results before using them, rather than trusting the first result found. 3. Chansa found two different dates online for when a particular Zambian nationalist leader was born, and simply chose the first one without checking further. Explain to Chansa TWO better steps she should have taken. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: For a class project, you have been asked to use a digital resource to find new information about a National Heritage Site in Zambia that you have not yet studied in detail, and to present your findings to the class. While searching online, you find two websites giving slightly different information about when the site was officially declared a National Monument. Task 1: Describe the steps you would follow to search for and record information about the heritage site. (7 marks) Task 2: Explain how you would handle the conflicting information found on the two websites. (7 marks) Task 3: Explain ONE way presenting your findings digitally (e.g. using a simple slide or typed handout) could benefit your classmates compared to only speaking from memory. (6 marks)

Assign: "Using any available digital resource (phone, computer, radio, or if none is available, by asking someone who has used one), find and write down ONE new fact about a Zambian historical topic of your choice, stating clearly where you found the information."

1. Recap: "Using digital resources to learn about the past requires a clear search process and careful evaluation of the reliability of what is found, just like any other historical source." 2. Preview: "Next, we will review and consolidate everything learnt in Topic 1.1 Introduction to History, before moving on to Topic 1.2 Measuring Time in History."
Mentioning historical durations: year and decade.
General Competence: Analytical Thinking
General Competence: Communication
Specific Competence 1.2.1.1: Explore patterns of historical durations.

Show learners a 2026 Zambian calendar and ask: "How many years have passed since Zambia got her independence in 1964?" Write the year 2026 and 1964 on the chalkboard. Ask: "Besides a 'year', what other word do we use for a period of ten years?" State the lesson goal: "Today we learn about a year and a decade as units of measuring time in History."

1. Define a Year: Explain that a year is the time it takes the earth to move once around the sun, made up of 365 days (366 in a leap year). Write the definition on the chalkboard. 2. Define a Decade: Explain that a decade is a period of ten (10) years. Write the definition on the chalkboard. 3. Zambian Examples: A year - the year Chipolopolo won AFCON (2012). A decade - the decade between 2010 and 2019 saw the construction of many roads under the Link Zambia 8000 project. 4. Group Activity: Put learners in groups of five. Give each group manila paper. Ask them to list 3 important events that happened in Zambia in specific years, and to identify which decade each event falls into (e.g. Mulungushi Rock of Authority declared a National Monument in 1971 - the 1970s decade). 5. Real-Life Application: Ask learners to state the decade of their own birth (e.g. a learner born in 2012 was born in the 2010s decade). 6. Synthesis: Summarise the definitions of a year and a decade on the chalkboard using Fig 2.1.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. Define the term 'year'. 2. Define the term 'decade'. 3. Mulenga, a Form 1 pupil at Kabulonga Boys Secondary School in Lusaka, says a decade and a year are the same thing because both are used to count time. Using your definitions, explain to Mulenga TWO reasons why this statement is not correct. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: You are the Class Monitor of Form 1B at Chinsali Day Secondary School in Muchinga Province. Your History teacher, Mr. Bwalya, has asked you to help younger learners understand time periods before a school heritage quiz. Task 1: Explain to the learners what a year is. (2 marks) Task 2: Explain to the learners what a decade is. (2 marks) Task 3: Give ONE Zambian historical example that took place within the decade 1960-1969. (2 marks)

Assign: "Ask a parent, guardian or grandparent in your home area (e.g. Chinsali, Mkushi or Kabwe) to tell you one important family event and the year it happened. Write the year and state which decade it falls into."

1. Recap: "A year is the time the earth takes to go round the sun once (365 days); a decade is a period of ten years." 2. Preview: "Next, we will learn about a generation and a century as further units of measuring time in History."
Mentioning historical durations: generation, century and millennium.

Ask learners: "How many years separate you from your grandparents in age, roughly?" Draw a simple three-level family tree on the board: Grandparent - Parent - Learner. Ask: "What word describes the gap between each level of this family tree?" State the lesson goal: "Today we learn about a generation, a century and a millennium."

1. Define a Generation: Explain that a generation is the average period, roughly 25-30 years, between the birth of parents and the birth of their children. Write the definition on the chalkboard. 2. Define a Century: Explain that a century is a period of one hundred (100) years. Example: the 20th century (1901-2000) saw Zambia gain independence. 3. Define a Millennium: Explain that a millennium is a period of one thousand (1000) years. Example: we are currently living in the 3rd millennium (2001-3000). 4. Group Activity: In groups of five, learners use the family tree resource to identify three generations in their own family (grandparent, parent, self) and estimate the number of years between each generation. 5. Real-Life Applications: Generation - the generation of freedom fighters such as Kenneth Kaunda and Simon Kapwepwe who fought for Zambia's independence. Century - the 21st century, which Zambia is currently in. Millennium - the transition from the 2nd to the 3rd millennium was celebrated in Zambia on 1 January 2000. 6. Synthesis: Summarise all five units learnt over the two lessons (year, decade, generation, century, millennium) using Fig 2.1.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. Define the term 'generation'. 2. Define the term 'century'. 3. Chanda, a Form 1 pupil at Nkrumah Secondary School in Livingstone, says the 20th century covers the years 2000 to 2100. Explain to Chanda why this statement is not correct, using your knowledge of centuries. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: You are preparing a short presentation for the Heritage Club at your school, Barotse Secondary School in Mongu. The Club Patron has asked you to explain the difference between a generation, a century and a millennium to new members using family and national examples. Task 1: Explain what a generation is, using an example from your own family. (3 marks) Task 2: Explain what a century is, using an example from Zambian history. (3 marks) Task 3: Explain what a millennium is, using the year 2000 as your example. (2 marks)

Assign: "Draw your own three-generation family tree (grandparent, parent, you) showing the approximate birth year of each person and the number of years between each generation. Use real names from your family in Zambia."
1. Recap: "A generation is about 25-30 years; a century is 100 years; a millennium is 1000 years." 2. Preview: "Next, we will learn how to calculate the number of years in a given historical period."
Calculating number of years in a given period.
General Competence: Critical Thinking

Ask learners: "Zambia became independent in 1964. This year is 2026. How many years has Zambia been independent?" Allow a few learners to attempt the calculation mentally. Write the correct subtraction on the board: 2026 - 1964 = 62 years. State the lesson goal: "Today we learn how to calculate the number of years between two given dates."

1. Explain the Rule: To find the number of years between two dates in the same era (both AD/CE), subtract the earlier year from the later year. 2. Worked Example 1: Kenneth Kaunda was born in 1924 and died in 2021. How many years did he live? 2021 - 1924 = 97 years. 3. Worked Example 2: The Mulungushi Rock of Authority was declared a National Monument in 1971. How many years ago was that, counting from 2026? 2026 - 1971 = 55 years. 4. Worked Example 3 (period between two past dates): The Central African Federation existed from 1953 to 1963. How many years did it last? 1963 - 1953 = 10 years. 5. Group Activity: In pairs, learners are given five date-pairs on manila paper (e.g. UNIP formed in 1959 and Zambia's first Republic ended in 1972; find the duration) and calculate the number of years for each. 6. Synthesis: Review the pair answers as a class and correct any errors, emphasising the subtraction rule.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. Calculate the number of years between 1911 (formation of Northern Rhodesia) and 2026. 2. Calculate the number of years the Central African Federation lasted, from 1953 to 1963. 3. Mutinta says that to find the number of years between 1964 and 2026, you must add the two numbers together. Explain to Mutinta why this method is incorrect and show her the correct method. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: You are a member of the History Club at Chipata Day Secondary School in Eastern Province. The club is preparing a wall display for the school's founding anniversary. The school was founded in 1962 and this year is 2026. Task 1: Calculate how many years the school has been in existence. (3 marks) Task 2: If the school plans a Golden Jubilee (50 years) celebration, in which year should this have taken place? (3 marks) Task 3: Explain why it is important for a school to know and celebrate such historical milestones. (4 marks)
Assign: "Find out the year your school (or a school near your home, e.g. in Mansa, Solwezi or Choma) was founded. Calculate how many years it has existed up to 2026."

1. Recap: "To calculate the number of years between two dates in the same era, subtract the earlier year from the later year." 2. Preview: "Next, we will learn how to convert a given year into its correct century."
Converting a year into a century.
General Competence: Problem Solving

Ask: "In which century do you think 1964, the year of Zambia's independence, falls?" Take a few guesses from learners (some may say 19th century, others 20th). Reveal the correct answer is the 20th century, and explain that today's lesson will show them why. State the lesson goal: "Today we learn how to convert any year into its correct century."

1. Explain the Rule: To convert a year into a century, add 1 to the first two digits of the year (drop the last two digits first). For example, for 1964: take '19', add 1, giving the 20th century. 2. Special Case: If the year ends in '00' (e.g. 1900, 2000), do NOT add 1; the year belongs to the century shown by its first two digits, e.g. 1900 is the 19th century, 2000 is the 20th century. 3. Worked Example 1: 1889 (the British South Africa Company received its Royal Charter) - first two digits '18', add 1 = 19th century. 4. Worked Example 2: 2021 (UPND won general elections) - first two digits '20', add 1 = 21st century. 5. Worked Example 3 (special case): 1800 - first two digits '18', ends in 00, so it remains the 18th century (no addition). 6. Group Activity: In groups of five, learners use Fig 2.2 and a list of 8 Zambian/world dates (e.g. 1911 formation of Northern Rhodesia, 1953 Central African Federation, 2000 Millennium celebrations, 1700 pre-colonial era) to convert each into its correct century. 7. Synthesis: Review answers as a class, correcting the common error of forgetting to add 1.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. Convert the year 1924 (birth of Kenneth Kaunda) into its correct century. 2. Convert the year 2000 into its correct century, explaining why the special rule applies. 3. Bupe insists that the year 1964 falls in the 19th century because it 'starts with 19'. Explain to Bupe why this reasoning is incorrect. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: You are helping to design a school History quiz board at Roma Girls Secondary School in Lusaka for the upcoming Heritage Week. The quiz includes a 'Guess the Century' round with important dates from Zambian and world history. Task 1: State the century for the year 1911 (formation of Northern Rhodesia) and show your working. (3 marks) Task 2: State the century for the year 1889 (BSA Company Charter) and show your working. (3 marks) Task 3: Explain why understanding centuries is useful when studying History. (4 marks)
Assign: "List the birth year of five members of your family or community in Zambia and convert each birth year into its correct century."

1. Recap: "To convert a year into a century, take the first two digits and add 1, unless the year ends in 00." 2. Preview: "Next, we will learn about the importance of chronology and what the term chronology means."
Explaining the meaning of chronology.
General Competence: Communication
General Competence: Analytical Thinking
Specific Competence 1.2.2.1: Arrange series of related events in chronological order.

Write these three sentences on the board in the wrong order: 'Zambia held multi-party elections in 1991. Zambia became a Republic in 1964. Zambia adopted a one-party state in 1972.' Ask: "What is wrong with the order these events are written in?" Guide learners to notice that the events are not in the order they actually happened. State the lesson goal: "Today we learn what chronology means and why it matters in History."

1. Define Chronology: Explain that chronology is the arrangement of events in the order in which they occurred in time, usually from the earliest to the most recent. 2. Explain Its Importance: Chronology helps historians and learners to: understand cause and effect between events; avoid confusion when studying the past; see how society has changed over time; and construct accurate timelines. Example: understanding that the slave trade preceded colonial rule in Zambia helps explain why some communities were already weakened before colonisation began. 3. Demonstration: Using Fig 2.3, show how a person's life events (birth, starting school, joining secondary school, sitting examinations, joining college) must be placed in chronological order to make sense. 4. Group Activity: Give each group five strips of paper with mixed-up Zambian historical events (e.g. Bantu migrations, arrival of missionaries, colonial rule established, independence attained, multi-party democracy restored). Learners arrange the strips in chronological order on their desks. 5. Real-Life Application: Ask a volunteer to narrate their own school life so far, but deliberately out of order, then ask the class to correct the chronology. 6. Synthesis: Summarise the meaning and importance of chronology on the chalkboard.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. Define the term 'chronology'. 2. State TWO reasons why chronology is important in the study of History. 3. Kondwani says that in History, the order in which events are studied does not matter as long as all the facts are covered. Explain to Kondwani why his statement is incorrect. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: You are a member of the Debate Club at Kitwe Boys Secondary School on the Copperbelt. During a recent debate on 'Understanding Zambia's Past', one team argued that studying History without following chronology is just as effective as following it. Task 1: Explain what chronology means. (2 marks) Task 2: Give TWO reasons why chronology is important when studying History. (4 marks) Task 3: Using an example from Zambia's history, show what confusion could occur if events are studied out of chronological order. (4 marks)

Assign: "Write five events from your own life (e.g. birth, starting Grade 1, moving to a new home, joining secondary school, a memorable achievement) in the correct chronological order, with the year each happened."

1. Recap: "Chronology is the arrangement of events in the order they occurred; it helps us understand cause and effect and avoid confusion." 2. Preview: "Next, we will practise arranging real family and community events in chronological order."
Arranging identified prominent events in our family and community in chronological order.
General Competence: Collaboration

Ask learners: "Can anyone tell the class one important event that happened in their family, and roughly when it happened?" Invite two or three learners to share briefly. Ask: "How would we arrange several such family events if we wanted to write our family's History?" State the lesson goal: "Today we arrange prominent family and community events in chronological order."

1. Explain Family Events: Guide learners to identify types of prominent family events, e.g. births, marriages (weddings), funerals, graduations, family relocations. Write examples on the board. 2. Explain Community Events: Guide learners to identify prominent community events, e.g. the opening of a local clinic, the building of a road, a chief's installation, a community school's founding. Example: the installation of Chief Mpezeni in Chipata's Eastern Province, or the opening of Levy Mwanawasa Stadium in Ndola in 2011. 3. Demonstration: Using a sample family (the 'Zulu family' of Chingola), the teacher lists five events out of order on the chalkboard and models how to reorder them chronologically with the class's help. 4. Group Activity: In groups of five, learners each contribute one family event with its year, and the group arranges all contributed events into a single chronological family/community timeline on manila paper. 5. Real-Life Application: Learners identify one prominent event in their own community (e.g. Mkushi, Kasama, Livingstone) and state where it fits chronologically relative to other group members' events. 6. Synthesis: Groups present their chronological family/community event lists to the class.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. State TWO examples of prominent family events that can be arranged chronologically. 2. State TWO examples of prominent community events that can be arranged chronologically. 3. Chomba's family has five events: his parents' wedding (2005), his birth (2008), his grandfather's funeral (1998), his sister's graduation (2023), and the family's move to Ndola (2015). Arrange these events in the correct chronological order. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: You are the Secretary of the Community Development Club at your school in Samfya, Luapula Province. The Club has been asked by the local Ward Councillor to compile a short chronological record of important events in the community for the Ward's 20th anniversary celebration. Task 1: Name TWO types of events that should be included in a community's chronological record. (4 marks) Task 2: Explain why it is important for a community to keep a chronological record of its history. (6 marks)
Assign: "Interview an elder in your community (e.g. in Samfya, Choma or Mansa) and list THREE important events that happened in your community, with their years. Arrange them in chronological order."

1. Recap: "Family and community events, such as births, weddings, and the opening of local schools or clinics, can be arranged chronologically to build an accurate record of the past." 2. Preview: "Next, we will arrange national and international events in chronological order."
Arranging identified prominent events in our country and internationally in chronological order.
General Competence: Citizenship

Ask learners: "Which happened first: Zambia's independence, or the Central African Federation?" Allow a short discussion and note the different answers. Reveal the correct order (Federation 1953, Independence 1964) and explain that today's lesson will help them order such events correctly. State the lesson goal: "Today we arrange national and international events in chronological order."

1. National Events: List key Zambian national events on the board: Bantu migrations (from around 1500s), establishment of colonial rule (1924), Central African Federation (1953-1963), Independence (1964), One-Party State (1972), Return to Multi-partyism (1991). 2. International Events: List key international/world events: First World War (1914-1918), Second World War (1939-1945), Formation of the United Nations (1945), Formation of the Organisation of African Unity/African Union (1963/2002). 3.
