Demonstration: Model arranging a mixed set of five national and international events (e.g. First World War, Zambia's Independence, Formation of the UN, Second World War, Central African Federation) into a single chronological sequence. 4. Group Activity: In groups of five, learners are given ten printed cards (five national, five international events) and arrange all ten into one combined chronological sequence on manila paper. 5. Real-Life Application: Learners discuss how a national event (e.g. Zambia joining the Non-Aligned Movement) relates in time to an international event (e.g. the Cold War). 6. Synthesis: Review the correct combined chronological order as a class and correct any errors.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. State the year Zambia attained her independence and the year the Central African Federation was dissolved. Which came first? 2. Arrange the following in chronological order: Formation of the United Nations (1945); Zambia's Independence (1964); Establishment of colonial rule in Northern Rhodesia (1924); Second World War begins (1939). 3. Nchimunya says that because Zambia is a small country, its history has no connection to world events like the World Wars. Explain to Nchimunya, using ONE example, why this statement is incorrect. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: You are a member of the National History Quiz Team representing your school, Munali Secondary School in Lusaka, at a Provincial competition. One of the rounds requires teams to correctly sequence major national and international events on a timeline chart within two minutes. Task 1: Arrange the following four events in chronological order: Zambia's Independence (1964); Formation of the Central African Federation (1953); First World War (1914-1918); Zambia returns to multi-party democracy (1991). (4 marks) Task 2: Explain why quiz competitions such as this one are useful for learners of History. (4 marks) Task 3: Suggest ONE additional national or international event your team could add to strengthen the timeline chart. (2 marks)
Assign: "List FOUR important events in Zambia's national history and arrange them in chronological order, showing the year for each."

1. Recap: "National and international events, such as the Central African Federation, Zambia's independence, and the World Wars, can and must be arranged chronologically for accurate historical understanding." 2. Preview: "Next, we will learn about the different types of timelines used to display chronological information."
Discussing types of timelines: progressive, regressive and pictorial timelines.
General Competence: Analytical Thinking
General Competence: Creativity and Innovation
Specific Competence 1.2.3.1: Apply chronology in writing a timeline.

Draw a simple straight line with an arrow on the board without any labels. Ask: "What do you think this kind of drawing is used for in History?" Accept answers and introduce the term 'timeline'. State the lesson goal: "Today we discuss the different types of timelines: progressive, regressive and pictorial."

1. Progressive Timeline: Explain that a progressive timeline moves from the earliest event (past) to the most recent event (present), read from left to right. Example: 1964 Independence -> 1972 One-Party State -> 1991 Multi-partyism -> 2011 PF wins -> 2021 UPND wins. 2. Regressive Timeline: Explain that a regressive timeline moves from the most recent event (present) back to the earliest event (past), also often read left to right but with dates decreasing. Example: 2026 Today -> 2021 UPND wins -> 2011 PF wins -> 1991 Multi-partyism -> 1964 Independence. 3. Pictorial Timeline: Explain that a pictorial timeline uses pictures, symbols or icons instead of, or alongside, words to represent events, making it visually engaging. Example: using a small drawing of a graduation cap to represent 'graduation' on a personal timeline. 4. Demonstration: Using Fig 2.4, show learners real examples of all three timeline types using Zambian political history. 5. Group Activity: In groups of five, learners are given the same five events (e.g. their own school's key milestones) and asked to draw the events as (a) a progressive timeline, and (b) a regressive timeline, using manila paper. 6. Synthesis: Review group work, highlighting the difference in the direction of dates between progressive and regressive timelines.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. Define a progressive timeline. 2. Define a regressive timeline. 3. Look at the following timeline: 2026 -> 2011 -> 1991 -> 1964. Is this a progressive or a regressive timeline? Explain your answer. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: You are a member of the Art and History Club at Kabulonga Girls Secondary School in Lusaka. The Club has been asked to design a wall chart for the school library showing important events using pictures instead of long written text, to appeal to younger learners in Form 1. Task 1: Name the type of timeline that would best suit this purpose. (2 marks) Task 2: Explain TWO advantages of using this type of timeline for younger learners. (4 marks) Task 3: Suggest ONE historical event and a picture/symbol that could represent it on this timeline. (2 marks)
Assign: "Draw a simple pictorial timeline of four events in your life so far, using at least one picture or symbol for each event instead of only words."

1. Recap: "There are three main types of timelines: progressive (past to present), regressive (present to past), and pictorial (uses pictures/symbols)." 2. Preview: "Next, we will construct our own personal timelines using specified guidelines."
Constructing a personal timeline under specified guidelines.
General Competence: Communication

Ask learners: "If you had to summarise your life so far in five key moments, what would they be?" Allow two or three learners to mention one event each. Show Fig 2.5, the personal timeline template, and explain that today they will fill in a similar one for themselves. State the lesson goal: "Today we construct our own personal timelines using specified guidelines."

1. Guidelines for a Personal Timeline: (i) Draw a straight horizontal line with an arrow; (ii) Mark at least five points along the line; (iii) Write the year above each point; (iv) Write a short description of the event below each point; (v) Arrange events in chronological (progressive) order from left to right; (vi) Give the timeline a clear title. 2. Demonstration: Using Fig 2.5, model constructing a personal timeline for a sample learner, 'Natasha from Kasama', showing her birth, starting Grade 1, joining secondary school, a major achievement, and the present year. 3. Individual Practice: Guide learners, step by step, to draw their own timeline following the six guidelines, using a ruler for the straight line. 4. Peer Review: Learners exchange their draft timelines with a desk-mate and check whether all six guidelines have been correctly followed. 5. Real-Life Application: Encourage learners to include at least one uniquely Zambian personal milestone, e.g. attending a traditional ceremony such as the Kuomboka or N'cwala for the first time. 6. Synthesis: Display two or three volunteered personal timelines on the notice board and discuss what makes them accurate and well-presented.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. State THREE guidelines that should be followed when constructing a personal timeline. 2. Why should events on a personal timeline be arranged in chronological order? 3. Ba Chishala drew a personal timeline but forgot to write the years above each event. Explain why this is a problem, using what you know about the purpose of a timeline. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: Your school, Solwezi Trades Training Institute Secondary Section in North-Western Province, is holding a 'My Life Journey' exhibition for Form 1 pupils, where personal timelines will be displayed and marked as part of continuous assessment. Task 1: State THREE guidelines you would follow to construct an accurate personal timeline for this exhibition. (6 marks) Task 2: Explain why displaying personal timelines can help build learners' self-confidence and identity. (4 marks)
Assign: "Neatly redraw your personal timeline on a clean sheet of paper using a ruler and colours, ready to be displayed on the classroom wall."

1. Recap: "A personal timeline must have a straight line, at least five labelled events with years, arranged chronologically, and a clear title." 2. Preview: "Next, we will construct a timeline of historical events rather than personal events."
Constructing an events timeline under specified guidelines.
General Competence: Digital Literacy

Recall the previous lesson's personal timelines and ask: "How is a timeline of historical events different from a timeline of your own life?" Guide learners to see that an events timeline focuses on events that affect a wider group of people, not just one individual. Show Fig 2.6, a sample events timeline of Zambia's history. State the lesson goal: "Today we construct a timeline of historical events using specified guidelines."

1. Guidelines for an Events Timeline: (i) Choose a clear theme, e.g. 'Zambia's Road to Independence'; (ii) Research and select at least five key dated events related to the theme; (iii) Draw a straight line with an arrow; (iv) Plot events chronologically with years and short descriptions; (v) Use consistent spacing where possible; (vi) Add a title and, where useful, a picture or symbol for each event. 2. Demonstration: Using Fig 2.6, model the six key dates in Zambia's history (1889 BSA Company Charter, 1924 Colonial Rule Begins, 1953 Central African Federation, 1964 Independence, 1991 Multi-party Democracy, 2021 UPND Government). 3. Group Activity: In groups of five, learners choose one theme from a given list (e.g. 'Zambia's Sporting History', 'World Wars', 'Zambia's Presidents') and research/construct an events timeline with at least five dated events on manila paper. 4. Digital Application: Where phones/computers are available, learners may verify one date online or using a reference book to ensure accuracy before finalising their timeline. 5. Presentations: Each group presents their events timeline to the class, explaining the theme and the significance of each event. 6. Synthesis: Display the timelines around the classroom as a gallery, and summarise the six guidelines on the chalkboard.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. State THREE guidelines for constructing an events timeline. 2. How does an events timeline differ from a personal timeline? 3. Mumba constructed a timeline of Zambia's Presidents but placed Edgar Lungu before Rupiah Banda. Explain why this is incorrect and state the correct order. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: You are part of the Heritage Committee at Chalimbana Secondary School in Chongwe, tasked with creating a permanent wall timeline in the school corridor showing the key stages of Zambia's journey to independence, for all pupils to view daily. Task 1: State THREE guidelines you would follow to construct this events timeline. (6 marks) Task 2: Name TWO key events that must appear on this timeline, with their approximate years. (4 marks) Task 3: Explain how a permanent wall timeline like this can benefit the whole school community. (4 marks)

Assign: "Choose one Zambian province (e.g. Muchinga, Luapula or Western Province) and research THREE important historical events associated with it. Construct a short events timeline showing these events with their years."

1. Recap: "An events timeline follows a chosen theme, uses accurately researched dates, and displays events chronologically with a clear title." 2. Preview: "Next, we will describe the importance of a timeline in the study of History."
Describing the importance of a timeline.
General Competence: Critical Thinking

Ask learners to bring out their personal and events timelines from the previous two lessons. Ask: "Now that you have made two timelines, what have you found useful about using a timeline compared to just writing a list of events?" Note a few responses on the board. State the lesson goal: "Today we describe why timelines are important in the study of History."

1. Reason 1 - Visual Clarity: A timeline presents information visually, making it easier to see the sequence and spacing of events at a glance compared to plain text. 2. Reason 2 - Shows Cause and Effect: A timeline helps learners see which events happened before others, helping to identify possible causes and effects, e.g. seeing that colonial rule (1924) came before the independence struggle (1950s-1964) suggests a cause-and-effect relationship. 3. Reason 3 - Aids Memory and Revision: Timelines act as a quick, memorable revision tool for examinations, since visual information combined with dates is often easier to recall than long paragraphs. 4. Reason 4 - Shows Duration and Pace of Change: A timeline shows how much time passed between events, helping learners understand whether change happened quickly or slowly, e.g. the rapid political changes in Zambia between 1990 and 1991. 5. Group Activity: In groups of five, learners examine their own constructed timelines from Lessons 9 and 10 and identify which of the four reasons above is best demonstrated by their own work, giving evidence. 6. Synthesis: Summarise the four reasons on the chalkboard and discuss any additional reasons learners suggest, e.g. timelines assist tourism guides at heritage sites such as the Livingstone Museum.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. State TWO reasons why timelines are important in the study of History. 2. Explain how a timeline can help a learner understand cause and effect between two events. 3. Chishimba says timelines are 'just for decoration' and are not really useful for serious History study. Explain to Chishimba why this statement is incorrect, giving TWO reasons. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: You are a Peer Educator at Malcolm Moffat Secondary School in Serenje, helping Form 1 classmates prepare for their end-of-term History test. Several classmates say they find it hard to remember the order of Zambia's key historical events. Task 1: Explain how constructing a timeline could help your classmates remember historical events better. (4 marks) Task 2: Give TWO other reasons, besides memory, why timelines are important in studying History. (6 marks)
Assign: "Write a short paragraph (5-6 sentences) explaining, in your own words, why you think timelines are useful, using your own personal or events timeline from previous lessons as an example."

1. Recap: "Timelines are important because they give visual clarity, show cause and effect, aid memory and revision, and show the duration and pace of change." 2. Preview: "Next, we will learn about the origins of man and views on the origins of man, but before that, we will study the abbreviations BC/BCE and AD/CE used to denote historical periods."

cbc_2023__hist__g1__1_2_measuring_time_i.subTopicName: 1.2.4 The Use of Abbreviations to Denote Historical Periods
notes: Explaining the meaning of abbreviations BC/BCE and AD/CE.
General Competence: Analytical Thinking
General Competence: Communication
Specific Competence 1.2.4.1: Use abbreviations BC/BCE and AD/CE to denote historical periods.

Write on the board: '500 BC' and '500 AD'. Ask: "Have you seen these letters before? What do you think they mean?" Allow learners to guess freely. Explain that these are abbreviations used worldwide, including in Zambian History textbooks, to show whether a date comes before or after a specific reference point in time. State the lesson goal: "Today we learn the meaning of BC, BCE, AD and CE."

1. Explain BC: BC stands for 'Before Christ', referring to the years before the traditionally accepted birth of Jesus Christ. 2. Explain BCE: BCE stands for 'Before Common Era', a religiously-neutral alternative to BC, referring to the same period of years before the reference point. 3. Explain AD: AD stands for 'Anno Domini', a Latin phrase meaning 'In the Year of our Lord', referring to the years after the reference point. 4. Explain CE: CE stands for 'Common Era', a religiously-neutral alternative to AD, referring to the same period of years after the reference point. 5. Key Point: BC/BCE and AD/CE refer to the same system of counting years; only the terminology differs (religious vs neutral). Both are accepted and used in Zambian and world History. 6. Group Activity: In groups of five, learners match four flashcards (BC, BCE, AD, CE) to their correct meanings and take turns explaining each to their group. 7. Synthesis: Summarise all four terms in a table on the chalkboard: BC = Before Christ; BCE = Before Common Era; AD = Anno Domini (Year of our Lord); CE = Common Era.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. What does the abbreviation 'BC' stand for? 2. What does the abbreviation 'AD' stand for? 3. Explain the difference between BC and BCE, and between AD and CE. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: You are assisting your History teacher, Madam Nyirenda, at Kasama Girls Secondary School in Northern Province, to prepare revision flashcards for Form 1 pupils ahead of a School-Based Assessment (SBA) test on Measuring Time in History. Task 1: Explain what BC and BCE mean. (4 marks) Task 2: Explain what AD and CE mean. (4 marks) Task 3: Explain why some modern textbooks prefer to use BCE and CE instead of BC and AD. (2 marks)
Assign: "Write out the full meaning of BC, BCE, AD and CE from memory, without looking at your notes, then check your answers against your exercise book."
1. Recap: "BC means Before Christ, BCE means Before Common Era, AD means Anno Domini (Year of our Lord), and CE means Common Era." 2. Preview: "Next, we will learn how to count years in BC and AD."
Counting years in BC and AD (BC count backward, AD count forward).
General Competence: Problem Solving

Ask learners: "Which year came first: 100 BC or 50 BC?" Allow different guesses and note them without correcting yet. Lay a rope on the classroom floor to represent a number line, with a marker in the middle for '0'. State the lesson goal: "Today we learn how to count years correctly in BC and AD."

1. Explain the AD Rule: AD/CE years count forward, meaning the further a year is from year 0/1, the larger the number and the more recent the date. Example: AD 500 is more recent than AD 100; 2026 AD (today) is more recent than both. 2. Explain the BC Rule: BC/BCE years count backward, meaning the further a year is from year 0/1, the larger the number, but the further back in the past (older) it is. Example: 500 BC is older (further in the past) than 100 BC, even though 500 is a bigger number. 3. Key Point: In BC, a SMALLER number is CLOSER to the present; in AD, a LARGER number is CLOSER to the present. 4. Demonstration on the Rope: Using the rope number line on the floor, place learners holding cards for 500 BC, 100 BC, 0, 100 AD and 500 AD in their correct physical positions, showing that 500 BC is furthest to the left (oldest) and 500 AD is furthest to the right (most recent). 5. Group Activity: In groups of five, learners are given six mixed BC and AD dates on cards (e.g. 44 BC, 1000 BC, 100 AD, 1964 AD, 753 BC, 2026 AD) and must arrange them physically or on paper from oldest to most recent. 6. Synthesis: Review the correct order as a class using Fig 2.7 and reinforce the key point about counting direction.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. Which came first: 753 BC or 44 BC? Explain your answer. 2. Which is more recent: AD 1000 or AD 1964? Explain your answer. 3. Kalaba says that because 500 is a bigger number than 100, 500 BC must be more recent than 100 BC. Explain to Kalaba why this reasoning is incorrect. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: You are a member of the History Society at Mongu Trades Training Institute Secondary Section in Western Province, helping to prepare a museum-style classroom display of ancient civilisations. The display includes cards for 3000 BC (Ancient Egypt), 753 BC (founding of Rome), and AD 476 (fall of the Western Roman Empire). Task 1: Arrange these three dates in chronological order, from oldest to most recent. (4 marks) Task 2: Explain, using the rule for counting BC years, why 3000 BC comes before 753 BC even though 753 is a smaller number. (4 marks) Task 3: Explain the general rule for counting years in AD. (2 marks)
Assign: "Arrange the following six dates from oldest to most recent: 1961 AD, 1200 BC, 44 BC, 2000 AD, 500 BC, 1500 AD."

1. Recap: "AD years count forward - a bigger number is more recent. BC years count backward - a bigger number is older." 2. Preview: "Next, we will practise using BC/BCE and AD/CE to correctly give a historical date."
Demonstrating the use of BC/BCE and AD/CE to give a date.

Write '1964' on the board and ask: "Should we write BC or AD after this date? Why?" Guide learners to see that 1964 (Zambia's independence) is after the birth of Christ, so it should be written 1964 AD (or simply 1964, since AD dates are often written without the abbreviation). Write '3000' on the board relating to Ancient Egypt and ask the same question. State the lesson goal: "Today we practise correctly writing dates using BC/BCE and AD/CE."

1. Writing Convention for BC/BCE: The abbreviation is written AFTER the number, e.g. 753 BC, 3000 BCE. 2. Writing Convention for AD/CE: AD is traditionally written BEFORE the number (e.g. AD 476), while CE is written AFTER the number (e.g. 476 CE). In everyday and Zambian school use, AD is also commonly written after the number for simplicity (e.g. 1964 AD). 3. Worked Example 1: The Rise of Ancient Egypt is dated to around 3000 BC (before the birth of Christ). 4. Worked Example 2: The fall of the Western Roman Empire happened in AD 476 (476 years after the birth of Christ). 5. Worked Example 3: Zambia's Independence is written as 1964 AD (or simply 1964, since it is understood to be an AD/CE date unless stated otherwise). 6. Group Activity: In groups of five, learners are given ten historical events with bare numbers (e.g. Julius Caesar assassinated, 44; Great Zimbabwe built, 1100; Zambia adopts new Constitution, 2016) and must correctly write each with BC or AD as appropriate. 7. Synthesis: Review the group answers as a class, correcting formatting errors (e.g. AD written after the number instead of before, where strict convention is taught).

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. Write the date 44 correctly using the appropriate abbreviation, given that Julius Caesar was assassinated in that year, before the birth of Christ. 2. Write the date 1885 correctly using the appropriate abbreviation, given that the Berlin Conference took place in that year, after the birth of Christ. 3. Explain the correct placement of the abbreviation 'AD' compared to the abbreviation 'BC' when writing a date. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: You are helping to design a labelled classroom History timeline poster at Chipembi Girls Secondary School in Chibombo District. Your teacher has given you a list of unlabelled dates and asked you to correctly format each with BC or AD before the poster is printed. Task 1: Correctly write the date for the founding of Rome, which took place 753 years before the birth of Christ. (2 marks) Task 2: Correctly write the date for Zambia's return to multi-party democracy, which took place 1991 years after the birth of Christ. (2 marks) Task 3: Explain why it is important to correctly label dates with BC or AD on a public poster like this one. (4 marks)
Assign: "Find FOUR historical dates from your History textbook or this syllabus (two BC dates and two AD dates) and write them out correctly using the proper abbreviation and placement."

1. Recap: "BC is written after the number (e.g. 753 BC); AD is traditionally written before the number (e.g. AD 476), though it is often written after in everyday use." 2. Preview: "Next, we will learn how to calculate the number of years between two given periods of time, starting with dates within the same era."
Calculating the number of years between two given periods of time: BC and BC; and BC and AD/CE.

Ask learners: "If an event happened in 100 BC and another happened in 50 BC, how many years passed between them?" Allow learners to attempt an answer using what they learnt about BC counting. Confirm the correct answer (100 - 50 = 50 years) and explain that today's lesson extends this skill further. State the lesson goal: "Today we calculate the number of years between two BC dates, and between a BC date and an AD date."

1. Rule 1 - Two BC Dates: Subtract the SMALLER BC number from the LARGER BC number (because the larger BC number is the older/earlier date). Example: from 753 BC (founding of Rome) to 44 BC (assassination of Julius Caesar): 753 - 44 = 709 years. 2. Rule 2 - A BC Date and an AD/CE Date: ADD the BC number and the AD number together, because the years span across the zero point in opposite directions. Example (Fig 2.8): from 500 BC to 300 AD: 500 + 300 = 800 years. 3. Worked Example 1 (BC to BC): From 3000 BC (Ancient Egypt) to 753 BC (founding of Rome): 3000 - 753 = 2247 years. 4. Worked Example 2 (BC to AD): From 44 BC (assassination of Julius Caesar) to AD 476 (fall of the Western Roman Empire): 44 + 476 = 520 years. 5. Group Activity: In groups of five, learners are given four date-pairs on manila paper (two BC-to-BC pairs, two BC-to-AD pairs) and calculate the number of years between each using the correct rule. 6. Synthesis: Review the group answers as a class, reinforcing when to subtract (same era) and when to add (BC to AD/CE).

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. Calculate the number of years between 1200 BC and 753 BC. 2. Calculate the number of years between 500 BC and AD 100. 3. Mwaba says that to find the years between 44 BC and AD 14, you must subtract 14 from 44. Explain to Mwaba why this method is incorrect and show the correct method. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: You are part of the Ancient History research group at Kabompo Secondary School in North-Western Province, preparing a fact sheet on Ancient Civilisations for the school's Open Day exhibition. Your fact sheet includes two dates: the founding of Ancient Egypt's Old Kingdom (2686 BC) and the founding of Rome (753 BC). Task 1: Calculate the number of years between these two dates. (4 marks) Task 2: If a third civilisation began in AD 100, calculate the number of years between the founding of Rome (753 BC) and this civilisation (AD 100). (4 marks) Task 3: Explain why it is important to correctly calculate such durations for a historical exhibition. (2 marks)
Assign: "Calculate the number of years between the following pairs of dates: (a) 1000 BC and 500 BC; (b) 200 BC and AD 200; (c) 3000 BC and 1000 BC."

1. Recap: "To find years between two BC dates, subtract the smaller from the larger BC number. To find years between a BC date and an AD date, add the two numbers together." 2. Preview: "Next, we will calculate the number of years between two AD/CE dates, completing our study of measuring time in History."
Calculating the number of years between two given periods of time: AD and AD/CE (including mixed and complex calculations).

Ask learners: "How many years passed between Zambia's independence in 1964 AD and today, 2026 AD?" Allow learners to calculate quickly, recalling the rule from Lesson 3. Confirm the answer (2026 - 1964 = 62 years) and explain this is the same rule used for two AD dates. State the lesson goal: "Today we calculate years between two AD/CE dates and practise all three BC/AD calculation rules together."

1. Rule 3 - Two AD/CE Dates: Subtract the EARLIER AD/CE number from the LATER AD/CE number, exactly as with ordinary years. Example: from AD 476 (fall of Rome) to AD 1964 (Zambia's independence): 1964 - 476 = 1488 years. 2. Recap of All Three Rules: (i) BC to BC - subtract smaller from larger BC number; (ii) BC to AD/CE - add the two numbers; (iii) AD/CE to AD/CE - subtract earlier from later AD/CE number. Write all three rules in a summary chart on the chalkboard. 3. Worked Example 1: From AD 1911 (formation of Northern Rhodesia) to AD 1964 (Zambia's independence): 1964 - 1911 = 53 years. 4. Worked Example 2 (Mixed Practice - Applying All Rules): Learners are given three separate date-pairs, one of each type, and must identify which rule applies before solving: (a) 1500 BC to 500 BC [BC-BC: subtract]; (b) 100 BC to AD 100 [BC-AD: add]; (c) AD 1953 to AD 1964 [AD-AD: subtract]. 5. Relay Competition: Divide the class into teams. Each team races to correctly solve 12 mixed date-pair cards (a mix of all three types) on manila paper, applying the correct rule for each, within a set time. 6. Synthesis: Announce the winning team and review any commonly made errors, reinforcing the three-rule summary chart.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. Calculate the number of years between AD 1953 (formation of the Central African Federation) and AD 1991 (return to multi-party democracy). 2. Identify which rule (subtract or add) should be used for the following, and calculate the answer: from 200 BC to AD 200. 3. Chibale mixed up his working and calculated the years between AD 800 and AD 1200 by adding the numbers together, getting 2000 years. Explain to Chibale why this is incorrect and show the correct working. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: You are the Timekeeper for the History Quiz Finals at Baluba Girls Secondary School in Kitwe, where the final round requires contestants to correctly calculate the number of years between historical dates read aloud by the quizmaster within 30 seconds each. Task 1: A contestant is given the dates AD 1924 (colonial rule begins in Northern Rhodesia) and AD 1964 (Zambia's Independence). Calculate the number of years between them. (4 marks) Task 2: A contestant is given the dates 100 BC and AD 100. Calculate the number of years between them, showing which rule you used. (4 marks) Task 3: Explain why contestants must be careful to identify whether dates are BC or AD before choosing whether to add or subtract. (2 marks)

Assign: "Calculate the number of years between the following THREE pairs of dates, clearly stating which rule (add or subtract) you used for each: (a) AD 1972 and AD 1991; (b) 44 BC and AD 476; (c) 1000 BC and 1 BC."

1. Recap: "For AD to AD/CE, subtract the earlier from the later date, just like ordinary years. Always identify BC or AD first before deciding whether to add or subtract." 2. Preview: "Next, we will review and consolidate everything learnt in the topic Measuring Time in History, in preparation for a School-Based Assessment."

cbc_2023__hist__g1__1_3_the_origins_of_m.subTopicName: 1.3.1 Views on the Origins of Man
notes: Introducing the topic: meaning of "Origins of Man" and the different views that try to explain it.
General Competence: Analytical Thinking
General Competence: Communication
General Competence: Digital Literacy
Specific Competence 1.3.1.1: Analyse religious and scientific views on the origins of man.

1. Show learners three picture cards: (a) a church at Mkushi Boma; (b) a mosque in Lusaka; (c) a Kuomboka traditional ceremony of the Lozi people. 2. Ask: "Where do you think human beings came from? Have you ever asked your parents or grandparents this question?" 3. Explain that today people give different answers to this question depending on their religion, science lessons, or cultural traditions. 4. State the lesson goal: "Today we introduce the topic of the Origins of Man and identify the different views that try to explain it."

1. Explanation: Explain that "origins of man" refers to how and when human beings first came into existence on Earth. Write this definition on the chalkboard. 2. Explain that there are three broad views that try to answer this question: (i) the Religious View - based on sacred books such as the Bible and the Qur'an; (ii) the Scientific View - based on evidence such as fossils and the theory of evolution by Charles Darwin; (iii) the Traditional/Cultural View - based on the oral beliefs of different Zambian ethnic groups such as the Bemba, Lozi and Tonga. 3. Draw the concept map (Fig 1.5) on the chalkboard, showing the three views branching from "Origins of Man". 4. Group Activity: Put learners in groups of five. Give each group manila paper. Ask each group to write down anything they already know or have heard about how man came to exist, sorting their ideas under the three headings: Religious, Scientific, Traditional. 5. Real-Life Application: Explain that a Form 1 pupil at the school may attend church on Sunday, learn about evolution in a Biology/History lesson, and also hear traditional stories from grandparents in the village during holidays - all in the same week. 6. Synthesis: Summarise the three views on the chalkboard and explain that this topic will explore each view and compare them.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. Define the term "origins of man". 2. Name the THREE broad views that try to explain the origins of man. 3. Chomba, a Form 1 pupil at the school, says his grandmother's traditional story about how the Bemba people came to be is "not real history" because it is not written in a science book. Explain to Chomba TWO reasons why his grandmother's traditional view should still be respected and studied. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: You are a Form 1 History Club Patron at your school in Mkushi District. During a club meeting, two members almost quarrel: one insists that only what the Bible says about creation is true, while the other insists that only science is true, and each refuses to listen to the other. Task 1: Explain to the club members what is meant by "origins of man". (2 marks) Task 2: Name two views, other than the one each member is defending, that also try to explain the origins of man. (2 marks) Task 3: Suggest one way you, as Patron, would help the two members respect each other's views. (2 marks)

Assign: "Ask two people in your home area (e.g. Mkushi Boma, Chalata, or your home village) what they believe about how human beings first came to exist. Write down their two answers and state which of the three views (Religious, Scientific, Traditional) each answer belongs to."

1. Recap: "There are three broad views on the origins of man: religious, scientific and traditional. Each view answers the same big question in a different way." 2. Preview: "Next, we will look closely at the Christian account of the creation of man."
Describing the creation of man according to religion: the Christian (Biblical) account.
General Competence: Citizenship

1. Ask learners: "How many of you attend a church here in Mkushi District or during holidays at home? What do you remember being taught about how God created the world?" 2. Show the cover of a Bible and mention the Book of Genesis. 3. State the lesson goal: "Today we describe the Christian account of the creation of man."

1. Explanation: Using the Book of Genesis Chapters 1-2, narrate the Christian account: God created the heavens, earth and light; then the sky, seas, land, plants; then the sun, moon and stars; then birds and sea creatures; then land animals; and finally God formed Adam from the dust of the ground and breathed the breath of life into him; Eve was later created from one of Adam's ribs to be his companion. 2. Draw/display the flow diagram (Fig 1.6) showing the stages of creation on the chalkboard. 3. Key Words: Guide learners to identify key words: "dust", "breath of life", "image of God", "rib", "Garden of Eden", "dominion". 4. Group Activity: In groups of five, learners re-tell the Christian creation account in their own words using the flow diagram as a guide, then present a summary to the class. 5. Real-Life Application: Relate the account to a Sunday sermon a learner may have heard at a church in Mkushi or Kabwe, where a pastor explains that human beings are made "in the image of God" and therefore deserve respect and dignity. 6. Synthesis: Summarise the account and its key message (that God is the Creator and gave man a special place above other creatures) on the chalkboard.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. According to the Christian (Genesis) account, what was Adam formed from? 2. How was Eve created according to the Christian account? 3. Mutinta, a Form 1 pupil at the school, says the Christian account and the story her grandmother in Serenje told her are "exactly the same". Explain to Mutinta ONE way the Christian account is different from a typical traditional Zambian account of creation. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: You have been asked by your Religious Education teacher at the school to prepare a short talk for Form 1 assembly on the Christian view of how man was created, because some pupils confuse the order of events. Task 1: Describe how God created Adam according to the Book of Genesis. (3 marks) Task 2: Describe how Eve was created. (3 marks) Task 3: Explain one lesson Zambians can learn today from the idea that man was made "in the image of God". (4 marks)

Assign: "Visit or recall a church service you have attended in your home area (e.g. Mkushi, Kabwe, Ndola). Write a short paragraph in your own words describing how that church teaches the story of the creation of man."

1. Recap: "According to the Christian account, God created the world in stages and finally formed man from dust and woman from man's rib, giving mankind a special place in creation." 2. Preview: "Next, we will look at the Islamic account of the creation of man."
Describing the creation of man according to religion: the Islamic (Qur'anic) account.

1. Ask: "Do any of you have a Muslim neighbour, classmate, or relative here in Mkushi District, Lusaka or the Eastern Province? What do you know about their beliefs?" 2. Show the cover of a Qur'an and explain that Islam also has an account of how man was created. 3. State the lesson goal: "Today we describe the Islamic account of the creation of man."

1. Explanation: Narrate the Islamic account: Allah announced to the angels His intention to place a vicegerent (Khalifa) on Earth; Allah formed Adam from clay/dust and shaped him; Allah breathed His spirit (Ruh) into Adam, giving him life; Allah commanded the angels to bow to Adam in respect, and all obeyed except Iblis (Satan), who refused out of pride and was cast out; Hawwa (Eve) was created as Adam's companion. 2. Draw/display the diagram (Fig 1.7) showing the stages of the Islamic account on the chalkboard. 3. Key Words: Guide learners to identify key words: "clay", "vicegerent/Khalifa", "Ruh (spirit)", "Iblis", "Hawwa". 4. Group Activity: In groups of five, learners compare the key words of the Islamic account to those of the Christian account learnt in Lesson 2 (e.g. "clay" versus "dust"; "Ruh" versus "breath of life"). 5. Real-Life Application: Relate the account to a real Zambian example, such as the annual Eid celebrations held by Muslim communities in Lusaka and other towns, where the Imam may remind worshippers that mankind is Allah's vicegerent responsible for taking care of the Earth. 6. Synthesis: Summarise the Islamic account and its key message (that man is Allah's vicegerent on Earth with a duty to care for it) on the chalkboard.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. According to the Islamic account, what was Adam formed from? 2. Name the angel/being who refused to bow to Adam and was cast out. 3. Bwalya, a Form 1 pupil at the school, says he has never met a Muslim before and thinks Islam has "nothing in common" with Christianity. Explain to Bwalya TWO similarities between the Islamic and Christian accounts of creation. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: The Civic Education and Religious Education Departments at your school in Mkushi District are organising an "Interfaith Awareness Week" to promote unity between Christian and Muslim pupils. You are asked to present on the Islamic view of the creation of man. Task 1: Describe how Adam was created according to the Qur'an. (3 marks) Task 2: Explain the meaning of the term "vicegerent (Khalifa)" as used in the Islamic account. (2 marks) Task 3: Suggest one way Interfaith Awareness Week can help promote national unity in Zambia. (3 marks)

Assign: "Find out from a Muslim friend, neighbour, or from research, one belief Islam holds about how human beings should treat the Earth, linking it to the idea of man as Allah's vicegerent. Write two sentences about it."

1. Recap: "According to the Islamic account, Allah formed Adam from clay, breathed His spirit into him, and made man His vicegerent on Earth, with Hawwa created as his companion." 2. Preview: "Next, we will directly compare the Christian and Islamic accounts of creation."
Comparing and contrasting the Christian and Islamic accounts of the creation of man.
General Competence: Critical Thinking

1. Ask learners to recall, in pairs, the main stages of the Christian account and the Islamic account learnt in the last two lessons. 2. Present a real scenario: "At the school, Chanda (a Christian) and Ibrahim (a Muslim) are classmates. Both believe God/Allah created the first man, but each tells the story slightly differently. Are their beliefs completely different, or do they share anything in common?" 3. State the lesson goal: "Today we compare and contrast the Christian and Islamic accounts of the creation of man."

1. Explanation & Demonstration: Draw a large Venn diagram on the chalkboard with two overlapping circles labelled "Christianity" and "Islam". 2. Similarities: Guide learners to identify features common to both, e.g. one Supreme Creator, man formed from soil/clay/dust, breath/spirit of life given by the Creator, woman created after man as his companion, man given a special status above animals. Write these in the overlapping middle section. 3. Differences - Christianity: God forms Adam from dust and breathes the "breath of life"; Eve is formed from Adam's rib; the account is found in the Book of Genesis in the Bible. 4. Differences - Islam: Allah forms Adam from clay and breathes "Ruh" (His spirit); Hawwa is formed as Adam's companion; angels are commanded to bow to Adam and Iblis refuses; the account is found in the Qur'an. 5. Group Activity: In pairs, learners copy the Venn diagram and sort five given statements (e.g. 'man is made from soil', 'the book is called the Qur'an', 'woman is formed from a rib', 'Iblis refuses to bow', 'one Creator is believed in') into the correct part of the diagram. 6. Synthesis: Review answers as a class and correct any misclassifications.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. State TWO similarities between the Christian and Islamic accounts of creation. 2. State TWO differences between the Christian and Islamic accounts of creation. 3. Namwene says, "Since Christians and Muslims believe in different books, they cannot be united as one nation." Using ONE similarity between the two accounts, explain why Namwene's statement is incorrect. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: You are a member of the Peace and Unity Club at the school. The club has been asked by the Head Teacher to prepare a wall display for the Guidance and Counselling Department showing how Christian and Muslim pupils at the school can live in harmony, using what they share in their belief about the creation of man. Task 1: State two features shared by the Christian and Islamic accounts of creation. (4 marks) Task 2: State two features that make the two accounts different. (4 marks) Task 3: Suggest one message the wall display should carry to promote unity between Christian and Muslim pupils at the school. (2 marks)

Assign: "Draw your own Venn diagram at home comparing any two beliefs or practices you know from two different religions or churches in your home area, e.g. a Catholic church and a Pentecostal church in Mkushi, or a church and a mosque."

1. Recap: "Christianity and Islam share important similarities, such as belief in one Creator and man being formed from soil, but differ in details such as their sacred books and specific events in the story." 2. Preview: "Next, we will begin to look at the scientific view of the origins of man, starting with Charles Darwin's theory of evolution."
Explaining the beginning of life on Earth according to scientists: Charles Darwin's Theory of Evolution (natural selection).

1. Show picture cards of a local Zambian village chicken and a commercial broiler chicken. Ask: "Why do you think these two chickens look so different, yet both are chickens?" 2. Introduce Charles Darwin as a British scientist who studied how living things change over time. 3. State the lesson goal: "Today we explain the scientific view of the beginning of man through Charles Darwin's Theory of Evolution."

1. Explanation: Explain that Charles Darwin, in his book "On the Origin of Species" (1859), proposed that all living things, including human beings, evolved (changed gradually) over millions of years from earlier, simpler life forms through a process called Natural Selection. 2. Break down the five steps: (i) Variation - individuals in a species differ slightly from one another; (ii) Struggle for survival - there is limited food, space and mates; (iii) Natural Selection - individuals with traits best suited to their environment are more likely to survive; (iv) Reproduction - survivors reproduce and pass their favourable traits to offspring; (v) Evolution - over millions of years, the species gradually changes. 3. Draw/display the process diagram (Fig 1.9) on the chalkboard. 4. Real-Life Application: Use the example of cattle in Zambia's Southern Province: cattle with traits suited to surviving droughts (e.g. tolerance to heat) are more likely to survive and reproduce, passing on those traits over many generations - this is natural selection at work, similar to what Darwin observed with finches on the Galapagos Islands. 5. Group Activity: In groups of five, learners use the five steps to explain, in their own words, why long-necked giraffes may have become more common than short-necked ones over millions of years (a classic evolution example), presenting their explanation to the class. 6. Synthesis: Summarise the theory: according to science, man did not appear suddenly, but evolved gradually over a very long period of time from earlier life forms.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. Name the scientist associated with the Theory of Evolution by Natural Selection, and name his famous book. 2. Arrange the following in the correct order according to Darwin's theory: Evolution, Variation, Natural Selection, Reproduction, Struggle for survival. 3. Kondwani, a Form 1 pupil at the school, says evolution means "a monkey woke up one day and turned into a human being". Explain to Kondwani TWO reasons why this statement is not an accurate description of Darwin's theory. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: You are a member of the Science and History Club at the school. The club has been invited to explain Charles Darwin's Theory of Evolution to Form 1 pupils at a nearby school in Serenje, some of whom have never heard of it. Task 1: Explain what is meant by "natural selection". (3 marks) Task 2: Using an example of livestock reared in Zambia (e.g. cattle or chickens), explain how natural selection could work in practice. (4 marks) Task 3: Explain one reason why scientists like Charles Darwin believe evolution takes millions of years rather than happening quickly. (3 marks)

Assign: "Observe animals kept at your home in Mkushi or your home village (e.g. chickens, goats, cattle, dogs). Write two sentences explaining one trait/feature that helps a particular animal survive better in your local environment, and explain how this relates to natural selection."

1. Recap: "According to Charles Darwin's Theory of Evolution, living things, including human beings, change gradually over millions of years through variation, struggle for survival, natural selection and reproduction." 2. Preview: "Next, we will look at the scientific evidence for human evolution, including fossils and the different stages of early man."
Explaining the scientific evidence and stages of human evolution (fossils and early hominids).

1. Ask: "If a scientist finds old bones buried deep in the ground near the Kalambo Falls in Zambia, how might they use them to learn about the past?" 2. Explain that scientists use fossils (preserved remains of ancient living things) as evidence to study how humans evolved. 3. State the lesson goal: "Today we explain the scientific evidence and stages of human evolution."

1. Explanation: Explain that scientists rely mainly on fossils (bones, skulls, teeth and tools preserved in rock over long periods) found at archaeological sites around the world, including sites near the Kalambo Falls and the Zambezi source area in Zambia and at Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania, to reconstruct the story of human evolution. 2. Present the four main stages: (i) Australopithecus (about 4 million years ago) - ape-like, but walked upright; (ii) Homo Habilis ('Handy Man', about 2.4 million years ago) - used simple stone tools; (iii) Homo Erectus ('Upright Man', about 1.9 million years ago) - used fire, had a larger brain; (iv) Homo Sapiens ('Wise Man', modern humans, about 300,000 years ago) - developed agriculture, art and language. 3. Draw/display the evolution stages diagram (Fig 1.10) on the chalkboard. 4. Group Activity: In groups of five, learners create a simple timeline chart on manila paper showing the four stages in order, with one feature written under each stage. 5. Real-Life Application: Mention that important fossil discoveries relevant to Zambia's own Stone Age heritage include the Broken Hill Skull (Kabwe Man), discovered at Kabwe in 1921, which is one of the most important early human fossils found in Africa, believed to be about 300,000 years old (this links forward to Topic 1.4: Stone Age). 6. Synthesis: Summarise the four stages and remind learners that the discovery of the Broken Hill Skull shows that Zambia itself is an important site for studying human evolution.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. What is a fossil, and how is it used by scientists? 2. Name the four main stages of human evolution in the correct chronological order. 3. Chalwe, a Form 1 pupil at the school, doubts that Zambia has any connection to human evolution, believing it is "something that only happened in other countries". Explain to Chalwe why this is incorrect, using ONE Zambian example. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: The National Heritage Conservation Commission of Zambia is planning an exhibition at a museum in Lusaka to showcase Zambia's role in the scientific study of human evolution, and has invited History pupils from the school to help design an information poster. Task 1: Name and briefly describe two stages in human evolution identified by scientists. (6 marks) Task 2: Explain the importance of the Broken Hill Skull (Kabwe Man) discovered in Zambia. (6 marks) Task 3: Suggest one way such a museum exhibition could benefit young Zambians. (8 marks)
Assign: "Find out more about the Broken Hill Skull (Kabwe Man) - where exactly it was found, when, and why it is important. Write a short paragraph about it."

1. Recap: "Scientists use fossil evidence, such as the Broken Hill Skull found at Kabwe in Zambia, to trace human evolution through stages: Australopithecus, Homo Habilis, Homo Erectus and Homo Sapiens." 2. Preview: "Next, we will look at the scientific explanation of the beginning of life on Earth as a whole, before human beings appeared."
Explaining the beginning of life on Earth according to scientists (from the formation of the Earth to the appearance of modern humans).

1. Ask: "If someone told you the Earth itself is billions of years old, much older than human beings, would you believe them? Why?" 2. Explain that today's lesson looks at how scientists explain the beginning of life on Earth as a whole, not just human beings. 3. State the lesson goal: "Today we outline the scientific timeline of the beginning of life on Earth."

1. Explanation: Using a long rope/string stretched across the classroom or playground as a simple demonstration, mark points to represent: (i) the Big Bang, about 13.8 billion years ago, when scientists believe the universe began; (ii) the formation of the Earth, about 4.6 billion years ago; (iii) the appearance of simple, single-celled life in the oceans; (iv) the evolution of more complex organisms and animals over hundreds of millions of years; (v) the appearance of modern humans (Homo sapiens), about 300,000 years ago. 2. Draw/display the timeline diagram (Fig 1.11) on the chalkboard. 3. Emphasise scale: explain that if the whole history of the Earth were compressed into a single 24-hour day, human beings would only appear in the last few seconds before midnight - helping learners grasp how recent humans are compared to the Earth's total age. 4. Group Activity: In groups of five, learners re-order five jumbled event cards (Big Bang, Earth forms, simple life appears, complex animals evolve, modern humans appear) into the correct chronological order and paste them on manila paper. 5. Real-Life Application: Relate the timeline to a familiar Zambian example: just as the Zambezi River took an extremely long time to carve out the Victoria Falls gorge through erosion, scientists believe life on Earth also took an extremely long time to develop and change. 6. Synthesis: Summarise the scientific timeline, from the Big Bang to modern humans, emphasising the vast lengths of time involved.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. According to scientists, approximately how long ago did the Big Bang occur, and what does it mark the beginning of? 2. According to scientists, approximately how long ago did modern humans (Homo sapiens) appear? 3. Mumba, a Form 1 pupil at the school, argues that "since the Earth is billions of years old and humans only appeared very recently, human beings are not important in the history of the Earth". Explain to Mumba TWO reasons why this conclusion does not follow correctly from the scientific timeline. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: Your school in Mkushi District is preparing a Science and History Fair display titled "How Old is Our World?" to help pupils and parents understand the scientific view of the beginning of life on Earth. Task 1: Outline, in the correct order, the main stages scientists use to explain the beginning of life on Earth. (10 marks) Task 2: Explain why scientists believe modern humans appeared very recently compared to the age of the Earth. (5 marks) Task 3: Suggest one benefit of teaching this scientific timeline to Form 1 pupils. (5 marks)

Assign: "Using a piece of string or a strip of paper one metre long, mark on it (roughly, by estimation) where you think the Big Bang, the formation of the Earth, and the appearance of modern humans would fall if the string represented the whole history of the universe. Write one sentence explaining what you notice."

1. Recap: "According to science, the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago with the Big Bang, the Earth formed about 4.6 billion years ago, and modern humans only appeared about 300,000 years ago - a very small fraction of Earth's history." 2. Preview: "Next, we will directly contrast the religious and scientific views on the origins of man, focusing on their differences."
Contrasting religious and scientific views on the origins of man: key differences.

1. Ask: "Two pupils at the school, Natasha and Emmanuel, are having a friendly argument. Natasha says God created man directly, while Emmanuel says man evolved from earlier life forms over millions of years. Who do you think is correct?" 2. Allow a short show of hands/opinions, without judging either side. 3. State the lesson goal: "Today we contrast the religious and scientific views on the origins of man, focusing on their key differences."

1. Explanation & Demonstration: Draw a two-column chart on the chalkboard headed "Religious View" and "Scientific View". 2. Difference 1 - Basis: Religious view is based on faith and sacred texts (Bible, Qur'an); Scientific view is based on evidence such as fossils, DNA and geological data. 3. Difference 2 - Process: Religious view holds that man was created suddenly/directly by God/Allah; Scientific view holds that man evolved gradually over millions of years. 4. Difference 3 - Testing: Religious claims are matters of faith and generally cannot be tested in a laboratory; scientific claims can be tested, observed, and reviewed/revised by other scientists. 5. Difference 4 - Purpose vs process: The religious view mainly answers "why" human beings exist (purpose, meaning); the scientific view mainly answers "how" human beings came to exist (process, mechanism). 6. Display the contrast chart (Fig 1.12) and go through each row with the class. 7. Group Activity: In groups of five, learners are given real statements (e.g. "Man was formed from dust and given the breath of life"; "Homo Erectus used fire and had a larger brain") and must correctly classify each as belonging mainly to the Religious View or the Scientific View, giving a reason. 8. Synthesis: Summarise the four key differences and remind learners that recognising differences does not mean disrespecting either view.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. State ONE difference between the religious view and the scientific view regarding how man came to exist (process). 2. State ONE difference between the religious view and the scientific view regarding the type of evidence used. 3. Chishimba insists that because science uses testable evidence, religion is "not worth studying" in History class. Explain to Chishimba TWO reasons why the religious view is still important to study alongside the scientific view. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: A local radio station in Mkushi District has invited a panel of Form 1 History pupils from the school to explain to the public the difference between religious and scientific views on the origins of man, after a heated call-in debate among listeners. Task 1: State two differences between the religious view and the scientific view on the origins of man. (8 marks) Task 2: Explain why scientific claims can be tested while religious claims are generally matters of faith. (6 marks) Task 3: Advise the radio listeners on how they should relate to one another despite holding different views on this topic. (6 marks)

Assign: "Ask a parent, guardian, or teacher at home in Mkushi District which of the two views (religious or scientific) they personally believe explains the origins of man, and ask them to give ONE reason for their choice. Write down their answer and reason."

1. Recap: "The religious and scientific views differ in their basis (faith versus evidence), their explanation of the process (sudden creation versus gradual evolution), and the type of question each answers (why versus how)." 2. Preview: "Next, we will look at what the religious and scientific views have in common, despite these differences."
Contrasting religious and scientific views on the origins of man: points of similarity/convergence.

1. Recall the differences discussed in the previous lesson by asking two or three learners to state one difference each. 2. Ask: "Apart from their differences, can you think of anything that the religious view and the scientific view might agree on?" 3. State the lesson goal: "Today we look at what the religious and scientific views have in common."

1. Explanation & Demonstration: Draw a Venn diagram on the chalkboard labelled "Religious View" and "Scientific View". 2. Similarity 1: Both views try to explain the same big question - how human beings came to exist. 3. Similarity 2: Both views agree that man began in a simpler/more basic form and became more complex or attained a special status over time (in religion, man is given dominion/is made vicegerent after creation; in science, simple life forms gradually became the complex modern human). 4. Similarity 3: Both views shape how people understand themselves, their place in the world, and how they should relate to other living things and to each other. 5. Similarity 4: Both views are respected and studied seriously by historians, and both continue to influence societies (including modern Zambian society) today. 6. Group Activity: In groups of five, learners discuss and list at least two additional similarities they can think of, and present them to the class for verification. 7. Real-Life Application: Explain that some Zambians, including scientists and religious leaders, hold both views together, believing, for example, that God may have used a process similar to evolution to bring about human life - showing that the two views are not always seen as mutually exclusive. 8. Synthesis: Summarise all similarities identified and emphasise that recognising common ground helps build tolerance and reduces unnecessary conflict between people of different beliefs.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. State ONE similarity between the religious view and the scientific view on the origins of man. 2. Explain why recognising similarities between the religious and scientific views is important for national unity in Zambia. 3. Given the similarities and differences studied, explain to a younger learner at Mkushi Primary School, in TWO sentences, why it is possible for a person to respect both the religious and scientific views without necessarily choosing only one. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: The Guidance and Counselling Department at the school has noticed that some pupils have started mocking classmates who hold a different view (religious or scientific) on the origins of man, causing tension in class. You are asked, as a member of the History Club, to help resolve this. Task 1: State two similarities between the religious and scientific views on the origins of man. (6 marks) Task 2: Explain how these similarities can be used to reduce the tension among pupils. (7 marks) Task 3: Recommend one rule the class should adopt to ensure respectful discussion of this topic in future. (7 marks)

Assign: "Write a short paragraph titled 'What Religion and Science Agree On', using at least two similarities discussed in class, giving your own opinion on why this matters for unity in your school or community."

1. Recap: "Despite their differences, the religious and scientific views share important similarities: both try to explain how man came to exist, and both show man moving from a simpler state to a more complex or special one." 2. Preview: "Next, we will look at Zambian traditional/cultural views on the origins of man."
Describing Zambian traditional/cultural beliefs on the origins of man, as a third view alongside religion and science.

1. Ask: "Before missionaries brought Christianity and Islam to Zambia, did our ancestors have their own beliefs about how human beings came to exist?" 2. Explain that many Zambian ethnic groups, such as the Bemba, Lozi and Tonga, had (and some still hold) their own traditional beliefs about a Creator and the beginning of mankind. 3. State the lesson goal: "Today we describe Zambian traditional/cultural beliefs on the origins of man."

1. Explanation: Explain that most Zambian ethnic groups traditionally believed in a Supreme Being/Creator, even before the arrival of Christianity and Islam. Examples: the Bemba people traditionally referred to the Creator as Lesa; the Lozi people of Western Province believed in Nyambe as the Creator God who made mankind and taught early people important skills such as fire-making and farming; the Tonga people of Southern Province referred to the Supreme Being as Leza, closely linked to rain-making and the giving of life. 2. Draw/display the illustrative map (Fig 1.14) on the chalkboard, showing the common thread of belief in a Creator across different Zambian ethnic groups. 3. Group Activity: In groups of five (where possible, grouping learners of different home ethnic backgrounds together), learners share and record any traditional beliefs, proverbs, or stories about the origin of people known in their own family/home area, e.g. from Mkushi District's Lala/Swaka people or other areas represented in the class. 4. Real-Life Application: Relate this to National Heritage/Traditional Ceremonies (Topic 1.6), explaining that ceremonies such as the Kuomboka (Lozi), Ncwala (Ngoni), Likumbi Lya Mize (Luvale) or Umutomboko (Lunda) often include praise and reference to the Creator and the ancestors, keeping traditional beliefs about origins alive today. 5. Synthesis: Summarise that Zambian traditional beliefs form a third, valuable view on the origins of man that should be respected as part of the nation's cultural heritage, alongside the religious and scientific views.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. Name the traditional term used by the Bemba people to refer to the Creator. 2. State ONE Zambian traditional belief about the origins of man, other than the Bemba example. 3. Mwaba, a Form 1 pupil at the school, says traditional beliefs about the Creator are "outdated" and have no connection to modern Zambian life. Explain to Mwaba ONE way traditional beliefs about the origins of man are still visible in Zambia today. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: The Ministry of Tourism is planning a Cultural Heritage Week in Mkushi District to promote Zambia's traditional beliefs and ceremonies to both local and international visitors. You are part of a team of Form 1 pupils from the school selected to research and present on traditional beliefs about the origins of man. Task 1: Name and describe two Zambian ethnic groups' traditional beliefs about the Creator. (8 marks) Task 2: Explain the importance of preserving such traditional beliefs for Zambia's national heritage. (6 marks) Task 3: Suggest one activity Cultural Heritage Week could include to showcase these beliefs to visitors. (6 marks)

Assign: "Ask an elder or grandparent in your home area what they know about your own ethnic group's traditional name for the Creator or their traditional belief about how the first people came to be. Write it down in a short paragraph."

1. Recap: "Many Zambian ethnic groups traditionally believed in a Supreme Being/Creator, such as Lesa (Bemba), Nyambe (Lozi) and Leza (Tonga), forming a valuable third view on the origins of man that is part of Zambia's cultural heritage." 2. Preview: "Next, we will hold a class debate comparing the religious and scientific views on the origins of man."
Debating the religious and scientific views on the origins of man.

1. Write the motion on the chalkboard: "Science explains the origins of man better than religion." 2. Ask learners to raise hands: who agrees, who disagrees, who is undecided? 3. Explain debate rules briefly: each side gets equal speaking time, no shouting, respect the opponent's beliefs at all times. 4. State the lesson goal: "Today we debate on the religious and scientific views on the origins of man, using everything we have learnt this topic."

1. Explanation & Demonstration: Divide the class into a Proposing Team (Science explains it better) and an Opposing Team (Religion explains it better), with the rest as the Moderating Panel/Judges. 2. Give each team 8 minutes to prepare arguments using notes from Lessons 1-9 (Christian and Islamic accounts, Darwin's theory, fossil evidence, the timeline of life, similarities and differences). 3. Model one sample argument: "Science explains the origins of man better because its claims, such as the Broken Hill Skull found at Kabwe, can be tested and verified by other scientists, unlike religious claims which rely only on faith." 4. Conduct the debate: Proposing Team presents (3 minutes), Opposing Team presents (3 minutes), rebuttals (2 minutes each side), closing statements (1 minute each side). 5. Judging: The Moderating Panel scores each team on clarity, use of evidence, and respectfulness, using the score sheet. 6. Synthesis: Announce the outcome and summarise the strongest arguments from both sides on the chalkboard, emphasising that both religion and science offer valuable, complementary insights into a question that continues to be studied and discussed today.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. Write ONE argument in support of the motion 'Science explains the origins of man better than religion.' 2. Write ONE argument against the motion (i.e. in favour of religion). 3. After the debate, Simunji still insists that religion is "completely useless" because it cannot be proven in a laboratory. Using what was discussed in the debate, write a response correcting Simunji's view. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: Your school in Mkushi District has been invited to send a team to represent Central Province at a National Schools Debate Championship in Lusaka, with the motion 'Science explains the origins of man better than religion'. However, the same week has important end-of-term History continuous assessment for all Form 1 classes. The Head Teacher has asked the Debate Club to advise on how to balance both. Task 1: Argue for the importance of allowing pupils to attend the debate championship. (7 marks) Task 2: Argue for the importance of prioritising the History continuous assessment. (7 marks) Task 3: Propose one balanced solution that respects the importance of both activities. (6 marks)
Assign: "Write a half-page personal opinion essay titled 'What I Believe About the Origins of Man, and Why I Respect Other Views', using at least three points learnt in this topic."

1. Recap: "Both the religious and scientific views offer valuable, though different, explanations of the origins of man; a good historian studies both fairly and respects people who hold either view." 2. Preview: "Next, we will discuss how respecting different views on the origins of man promotes good citizenship in Zambia."
Applying knowledge of the different views on the origins of man to promote tolerance, respect and good citizenship in Zambia.
General Competence: Emotional Intelligence

1. Ask: "Have you ever seen or heard of someone being mocked or excluded because of their religious belief, their acceptance of science, or their traditional/cultural beliefs, here in Mkushi District or elsewhere in Zambia?" 2. Allow two or three learners to briefly share (without naming individuals) any such experience they may have witnessed. 3. State the lesson goal: "Today we discuss how respecting different views on the origins of man promotes tolerance and good citizenship."

1. Explanation: Explain that Zambia is a multi-religious, multi-ethnic nation with the national motto "One Zambia, One Nation", and that respecting different views on sensitive topics such as the origins of man is an important part of good citizenship. 2. Present the citizenship wheel (Fig 1.16) showing four values: (i) Respect for religious beliefs; (ii) Respect for scientific knowledge; (iii) Respect for cultural/traditional views; (iv) Tolerance and unity in diversity. 3. Role-Play Activity: In groups of five, learners are given short role-play cards describing a conflict scenario (e.g. a Form 1 pupil mocking a classmate's church belief; a pupil dismissing traditional beliefs as "backward"; a pupil rejecting a scientific explanation without listening). Each group acts out the scenario and then a peaceful, respectful resolution. 4. Discussion: After each role-play, the class discusses what values (from the wheel) were shown or missing, and how the situation could be better handled. 5. Real-Life Application: Relate the discussion to national events such as Zambia's National Day of Prayer, Fasting, Repentance and Reconciliation, and to interfaith and inter-cultural cooperation seen in Zambian public life, showing that respecting diverse views is part of Zambia's national character. 6. Synthesis: Summarise the four citizenship values from the wheel and their importance for a peaceful, united Zambia.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. State ONE citizenship value that helps learners respect people who hold a different view on the origins of man. 2. Explain why Zambia's national motto 'One Zambia, One Nation' is relevant to this topic. 3. During a class discussion, Nawa openly laughs at a classmate, Fweta, for believing the traditional Tonga account of creation instead of the scientific one. Explain to Nawa TWO reasons why this behaviour is wrong, and suggest what Nawa should do instead. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: The Guidance and Counselling Department, working with the History Department at the school, has been asked by the Provincial Education Office to design a short 'Unity in Diversity' campaign for Form 1 pupils across Central Province, using the topic of the origins of man as a starting point. Task 1: Explain how knowledge of the religious, scientific and traditional views on the origins of man can help promote unity among pupils of different backgrounds. (8 marks) Task 2: Suggest two activities the campaign could include to teach tolerance using this topic. (6 marks) Task 3: Explain one way such a campaign could benefit Zambia as a nation in the long run. (6 marks)

Assign: "Design a simple poster (on a sheet of paper) with the slogan 'Different Views, One Zambia', illustrating at least two of the views on the origins of man (religious, scientific, traditional) living together in unity."

1. Recap: "Respecting different views on the origins of man - religious, scientific and traditional - builds tolerance, reduces conflict, and strengthens the unity called for by Zambia's motto, 'One Zambia, One Nation'." 2. Preview: "Next, we will revise the whole topic and practise ECSEOL-style examination questions on the origins of man."
Revision and consolidation of Topic 1.3 (The Origins of Man), with practice of ECSEOL-style examination questions.

1. Ask learners to close their books and, as a whole class, quickly call out anything they remember from the topic so far (a "popcorn" recall activity). 2. List learners' responses briefly on the chalkboard without correcting yet. 3. State the lesson goal: "Today we revise the whole topic on the Origins of Man and practise ECSEOL-style examination questions."

1. Explanation & Demonstration: Display the completed revision mind-map (Fig 1.17), showing the four branches: Religious View, Scientific View, Zambian Traditional View, and Contrasts/Similarities, correcting and organising the learners' earlier "popcorn" list under the correct branch. 2. Explain the ECSEOL question style clearly: examination and continuous assessment questions are usually presented as a real-life scenario, followed by tasks (a), (b), (c) or Task 1, 2, 3, each carrying specific marks, and learners must apply their knowledge to the scenario rather than simply recalling facts. 3. Guided Practice: Work through one full ECSEOL-style scenario question as a class (see Exercise Question 4 below), modelling how to identify what each task is asking and how to structure a full-mark answer. 4. Group Activity: In groups of five, learners are given different revision question cards (one card per group, covering a different sub-topic: Christianity, Islam, Darwin's theory, fossil evidence/timeline, Zambian traditional views, or similarities/differences) to answer together and then present their answers to the class for checking. 5. Peer Marking: Groups exchange answers and mark each other's work using model answers provided by the teacher, building assessment literacy. 6. Synthesis: Recap the whole topic using the mind-map, and remind learners of the importance of reading each scenario carefully before answering in the examination.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. State the FOUR main branches of this topic as shown on the revision mind-map. 2. In the ECSEOL examination format, how are History questions usually presented, and how many tasks/marks does each scenario typically carry? 3. Explain briefly why it is important, before answering an ECSEOL-style scenario question, to read the scenario carefully and identify exactly what each task requires. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION (FULL PRACTICE ITEM - EoC1: Demonstrates understanding of the ideologies of Evolution and early civilisation): You are the Chairperson of the History Club at the school. The Provincial Education Office in Central Province has selected your club to host a Provincial Quiz Competition on 'The Origins of Man', where teams from schools such as Serenje Girls Technical School, Kabwe Secondary School and Ndola Girls Technical School will compete. As Chairperson, you are asked to prepare the official model answers for the quiz masters. Task 1: Describe how man was created according to EITHER the Christian OR the Islamic account. (7 marks) Task 2: Explain how Charles Darwin's Theory of Evolution suggests man came to exist. (7 marks) Task 3: Suggest two ways the quiz competition can help promote unity and tolerance among the participating schools from different parts of Zambia. (6 marks)

Assign: "Using your notes from all lessons on the Origins of Man, write your own ECSEOL-style scenario question (with a short real-life scenario and two tasks with marks) on any part of this topic, together with your own model answers. Be ready to exchange your question with a classmate next lesson."

1. Recap: "We have now covered the full topic of the Origins of Man: the Christian and Islamic religious accounts, the scientific view through Darwin's theory and fossil evidence, Zambian traditional beliefs, and how all these views compare and can be respected together as good citizens." 2. Preview: "Next, we move to a new topic: The Stone Age, where we will study the earliest known human societies and their way of life."

cbc_2023__hist__g1__1_4_stone_age__1_4_1.subTopicName: 1.4.1 The Way of Life in Stone Age
notes: Classifying the Stone Age into its three periods: Early Stone Age (Palaeolithic), Middle Stone Age (Mesolithic) and Late Stone Age (Neolithic).
General Competence: Analytical Thinking
General Competence: Communication
Specific Competence 1.4.1.1: Draw lessons from Stone Age way of life (Classifying the Stone Age).

Show learners a plain stone and ask, "What do you think our ancestors used a stone like this for, long before metal tools were discovered?" Explain that today's lesson goes back to the very beginning of human history, before iron working, to a time called the Stone Age. State the lesson goal: "Today we classify the Stone Age into its three periods."

Define the Stone Age: the earliest and longest period of human history when people made and used tools mainly from stone, before the discovery of metal. Explain that historians classify the Stone Age into three periods based on how advanced the stone tools were: Early Stone Age (Palaeolithic/Old Stone Age), Middle Stone Age (Mesolithic) and Late Stone Age (Neolithic/New Stone Age). Display the timeline (Fig 1.4a) and explain the approximate duration of each period. Zambian example: Early and Middle Stone Age tools have been found at Kabwe (Broken Hill) and Mumbwa Caves in Central Province, while Late Stone Age tools and rock art have been found at Nachikufu Caves near Mpika in Muchinga Province. Group Activity: In groups of five, learners draw their own timeline on manila paper, labelling the three periods and one Zambian site under each. Synthesis: Summarise the three periods and their alternative names on the chalkboard.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. Define the term Stone Age. 2. Name the three periods of the Stone Age. 3. Chomba, a Form 1 pupil at Kabulonga Girls Secondary School in Lusaka, argues that the Stone Age was "just one long period with no changes."
