Using what you have learnt, explain to Chomba TWO reasons why this statement is not correct. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: You are a member of the History Club at your school. The club has been invited to mount a small display for Heritage Week showing how early Zambians lived before farming and iron working began. Task 1: Explain to visitors what the Stone Age is. (4 marks) Task 2: Name and briefly describe the three periods of the Stone Age that your display should represent. (10 marks) Task 3: Suggest one Zambian site your club could use as an example for each period. (6 marks)

Assign: "Using a ruler, draw a timeline in your exercise book showing the three periods of the Stone Age in the correct order, and next to each period write one Zambian place where tools from that period have been found."

Recap: "The Stone Age is classified into the Early, Middle and Late Stone Age, based on how advanced the tools were." Preview: "Next, we will identify the actual human ancestor who lived during the Early Stone Age."
Identifying the human ancestor of the Early Stone Age — Homo Habilis.
General Competence: Critical Thinking
Specific Competence 1.4.1.1: Draw lessons from Stone Age way of life (Identifying the human ancestor of the Early Stone Age).

Ask learners to recall the three periods of the Stone Age learnt in the previous lesson. Show a drawing of an early human-like skull and ask, "Who do you think this creature is, and in which Stone Age period did it live?" State the lesson goal: "Today we identify and describe the human ancestor of the Early Stone Age."

Explain that the human ancestor commonly studied for the Early Stone Age is Homo Habilis ("Handy Man"), believed to be among the earliest tool-making ancestors, living roughly 2.6 million to 1.5 million years ago mainly in East and Southern Africa. Describe features: smaller brain than modern humans; walked upright on two legs; made simple, rough pebble tools (Oldowan tools) for cutting and pounding; lived in small family groups; gathered wild plants and scavenged meat. Zambian/regional link: Early Stone Age tool evidence associated with such early toolmakers has been found in the Broken Hill (Kabwe) area and other Central African sites, showing early humans occupied this region. Group Activity: In pairs, learners list THREE features that made Homo Habilis different from modern humans and ONE way Homo Habilis was similar to modern humans. Role Play: Two learners mime how an Early Stone Age person might use a pebble tool to cut meat or crack a bone, while classmates guess the activity. Synthesis: Summarise features of Homo Habilis on the board under two headings: 'Similar to us' and 'Different from us'.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. Name the human ancestor associated with the Early Stone Age. 2. State TWO features of Homo Habilis. 3. Musonda tells his young brother that "the first humans looked and lived exactly like people today." Using what you have learnt about Homo Habilis, explain TWO reasons why Musonda is wrong. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: You are a tour guide trainee at a museum in Livingstone that has a display on human origins. A group of visiting Form 1 pupils from Munali Secondary School in Lusaka asks you to explain the earliest tool-making humans. Task 1: Identify the human ancestor of the Early Stone Age and explain what the name means. (4 marks) Task 2: Describe THREE features of this ancestor's way of life. (10 marks) Task 3: Explain why studying such ancestors is important for understanding Zambia's history. (6 marks)
Assign: "Draw and label a simple picture of Homo Habilis using a stone tool, showing at least two features that make it different from a modern human."

Recap: "Homo Habilis, the 'Handy Man', was the human ancestor of the Early Stone Age, known for simple pebble tools." Preview: "Next, we will identify the human ancestors of the Middle and Late Stone Age."
Identifying the human ancestors of the Middle Stone Age (Broken Hill Man) and the Late Stone Age (Bushmen/San).
General Competence: Citizenship
Specific Competence 1.4.1.1: Draw lessons from Stone Age way of life (Identifying the human ancestors of the Middle and Late Stone Age).

Ask learners to recall Homo Habilis and the Stone Age period he belonged to. Narrate: "In 1921, miners at Broken Hill Mine in Kabwe, Zambia, discovered an old human skull while digging for lead and zinc. This skull became famous the world over." Ask: "Which Stone Age period do you think this skull might belong to?" State the lesson goal.

Explain that the Middle Stone Age human ancestor commonly studied is Broken Hill Man (also called Rhodesian Man / Homo rhodesiensis / Kabwe Man), whose skull was discovered at Kabwe, Zambia in 1921. Broken Hill Man had a larger brain than Homo Habilis and made improved, sharper stone tools. Explain that the Late Stone Age human ancestor commonly studied is the Bushmen (San people) - small hunter-gatherer communities known for fine, small stone tools (microliths), bows and arrows, and rock art, some of which can still be seen in Zambia at Mwela Rocks near Kasama and Nsalu Cave. Compare the two on the chalkboard: Middle Stone Age (Broken Hill Man) - improved tools, larger brain, found at Kabwe; Late Stone Age (Bushmen/San) - finest tools, rock art, found at Mwela Rocks and Nachikufu. Group Activity: Divide the class into two groups. Group A researches and lists facts about Broken Hill Man; Group B lists facts about the Bushmen/San, using notes and manila paper. Gallery Walk: Groups display and present their findings to the class. Synthesis: Complete a three-ancestor summary on the chalkboard: Homo Habilis (Early) - Broken Hill Man (Middle) - Bushmen/San (Late).

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. Where in Zambia was the skull of Broken Hill Man discovered, and in which year? 2. Name the Late Stone Age human ancestor known for fine tools and rock art. 3. A tourist visiting Kabwe asks Nchimunya, a Form 1 pupil, why the town is important in the history of human origins. Using what you have learnt, help Nchimunya give TWO correct reasons. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: You are a tour guide at a cultural centre near Kasama that displays rock art believed to have been made by the San people. A group of visiting researchers wants to understand the human story behind the site. Task 1: Identify the human ancestor group associated with the Late Stone Age rock art. (4 marks) Task 2: Describe THREE features of the way of life of this Late Stone Age ancestor. (10 marks) Task 3: Explain the importance of the Broken Hill Man discovery in Kabwe to Zambia's history. (6 marks)
Assign: "Interview an elderly family member or neighbour about any old rock paintings, caves or 'ancient stones' they know of in your area, and write three sentences about what they told you."

Recap: "The three human ancestors of the Stone Age are Homo Habilis (Early), Broken Hill Man (Middle) and the Bushmen/San (Late)." Preview: "Next, we will discuss the social aspects of life in the Stone Age."
Describing the social aspects of Stone Age life: family/band life, division of labour, communication and beliefs.
Specific Competence 1.4.1.1: Draw lessons from Stone Age way of life (Describing social aspects of the Stone Age).

Ask: "If you had no phone, no school and no shops, how would you and your family survive together?" Explain that Stone Age people lived in small family groups called bands, and today's lesson explores their social life. State the lesson goal.

Explain social organisation: Stone Age people lived in small bands/family groups of about 20-30 people, related by blood or marriage, who moved together in search of food. Explain cooperation and division of labour: men mostly hunted; women and children gathered wild fruits, roots and insects; all members cared for the young and the old; children learnt skills directly from parents and elders since there were no formal schools. Explain communication and beliefs: Stone Age people communicated using simple language and gestures, and expressed daily life and beliefs through rock art/paintings, e.g. at Mwela Rocks (Kasama) and Nsalu Cave. Real-life link: Compare to a modern Zambian extended family working together on a farm in, for example, Chibombo District, where every member has a role - showing that cooperation as a value has continued into today's society. Group Activity: In groups of five, learners role-play a 'Stone Age band' preparing for a day, assigning roles (hunters, gatherers, child-minders, tool-makers) and acting out a short cooperative scene on the school playground. Synthesis: List social features on the chalkboard under 'Family/band life', 'Division of labour' and 'Communication and beliefs'.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. What is a 'band' in relation to Stone Age social life? 2. State TWO ways men and women shared work in a Stone Age band. 3. Chalwe says people in the Stone Age "lived alone and cared only for themselves." Using what you have learnt about social life, explain to Chalwe why this is incorrect. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: Your school's Cultural and Heritage Club has been asked to perform a short skit for Independence Day, showing how early Zambians lived together as families before modern institutions like schools and hospitals existed. Task 1: Explain what a Stone Age 'band' was. (4 marks) Task 2: Describe THREE social practices your skit should show, such as division of labour and care for the young and old. (10 marks) Task 3: Suggest one way the skit could link Stone Age cooperation to values Zambians still practise today, such as community spirit. (6 marks)
Assign: "Write a paragraph describing how your own family or neighbours in your community cooperate and share duties today, and compare this to Stone Age band life."

Recap: "Stone Age people lived in family bands, shared work between men, women and children, and communicated through simple language and rock art." Preview: "Next, we will discuss the political aspects of life in the Stone Age."
Describing the political aspects of Stone Age life: leadership, decision-making and conflict resolution.
Specific Competence 1.4.1.1: Draw lessons from Stone Age way of life (Describing political aspects of the Stone Age).

Ask: "Who makes the big decisions in your home or community today, for example a Chief, a Headman or your parents?" Explain that even without governments, courts or police, Stone Age bands still had ways of leading themselves and settling disputes. State the lesson goal.

Explain leadership: Stone Age bands were led informally by the oldest or most experienced/skilled member (e.g. the best hunter or an elder), not by kings, chiefs or a formal government; leadership was based on ability and respect, not inheritance. Explain decision-making: important decisions, such as when to move camp or where to hunt, were made through discussion among the adult members of the band, similar to a small community meeting. Explain conflict resolution: disputes were settled informally through discussion or mediation by elders; in serious cases the band could split into smaller groups; there were no formal written laws, courts or police. Zambian real-life link: compare to how a village today, for example in Mkushi or Chinsali, may still settle small disputes through a Village Headman or Induna before involving formal police or courts, showing that informal leadership has continued in modified form. Group Activity/Role Play: In groups, learners role-play a 'band meeting' deciding where to move camp because water has dried up, showing discussion and consensus-building. Synthesis: Chalkboard summary - 'Leadership: skill/age-based; Decision-making: group discussion; Justice: informal, elder-mediated'.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. How were leaders chosen in a Stone Age band? 2. State ONE way disputes were settled in Stone Age bands. 3. Mumba argues that the Stone Age had "no leadership at all." Using what you have learnt, correct Mumba's statement with TWO points. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: The Civic Education and History Clubs at Ndeke Secondary School in Kabwe have been asked to compare early forms of leadership with leadership in Zambia today, for a Democracy Week debate. Task 1: Explain how leadership operated in a Stone Age band. (4 marks) Task 2: Describe THREE features of political/leadership life in the Stone Age, such as decision-making and dispute settlement. (10 marks) Task 3: Suggest one way modern Zambian society has improved on Stone Age methods of leadership and justice. (6 marks)

Assign: "Ask a parent or guardian how disagreements are settled in your home area, for example by a headman, church elder or community leader, and write two sentences comparing this to Stone Age conflict resolution."

Recap: "Stone Age bands were led informally by the most skilled or respected members, and decisions and disputes were handled through discussion rather than formal government." Preview: "Next, we will discuss the economic aspects of life in the Stone Age."
Describing the economic aspects of Stone Age life: hunting, gathering, fishing and simple exchange.
General Competence: Financial Literacy
Specific Competence 1.4.1.1: Draw lessons from Stone Age way of life (Describing economic aspects of the Stone Age).

Take learners to the school playground (or use the classroom) and ask them to find and collect three natural objects (leaves, seeds, small stones) within two minutes, as Stone Age gatherers would have done. Ask: "How did it feel searching for food or resources without a shop nearby?" State the lesson goal: "Today we discuss how the Stone Age economy worked."

Explain that the Stone Age economy was a subsistence economy, based on hunting, gathering and, in some areas, fishing - there was no farming, money or formal trade as known today. Explain hunting: men used spears, and later bows and arrows, to kill wild animals such as antelope for meat, skins and bones. Explain gathering: women and children collected wild fruits, roots, tubers, honey and insects, forming the largest part of the diet. Explain fishing: bands living near rivers and lakes such as the Kafue and Zambezi supplemented their diet with fish, caught using simple traps, spears or nets made from plant fibres. Explain sharing/exchange: food obtained was shared among all members of the band; some bands exchanged surplus items, such as skins and shells, with neighbouring bands - an early, simple form of exchange without money. Group Activity: In groups, learners create a 'menu for one day in the life of a Stone Age family' using Zambian wildlife/plant examples, e.g. impala meat, wild loquats (masuku), honey and Kafue bream, and complete the Fig 1.4c wheel diagram combining social, political and economic aspects.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. Name the THREE main economic activities of Stone Age people. 2. What is meant by a 'subsistence economy'? 3. Bupe insists that Stone Age people "had no way of getting food without shops." Using what you have learnt, correct Bupe with TWO points. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: You are a member of the Young Historians Club at a school near the Kafue River. The club wants to create an exhibition comparing how early Zambians near rivers survived economically with how communities along the Kafue River earn a living today. Task 1: Explain the term 'subsistence economy' as used in the Stone Age. (4 marks) Task 2: Describe THREE ways Stone Age people obtained food and resources. (10 marks) Task 3: Compare one Stone Age economic activity with a similar modern economic activity practised along the Kafue River today, such as fishing. (6 marks)

Assign: "Write a short paragraph listing THREE wild foods (fruits, plants, animals or fish) found in your area that Stone Age people might have relied on, and explain how people in your community use similar resources today."

Recap: "Stone Age people survived through a subsistence economy based on hunting, gathering, fishing and simple sharing/exchange." Preview: "Next, we will analyse the tools that Stone Age people used for hunting, cutting and digging."
Analysing the use of various Stone Age tools: hunting, cutting and digging tools.
General Competence: Digital Literacy
Specific Competence 1.4.1.1: Draw lessons from Stone Age way of life (Analysing the use of various Stone Age tools).

Pass around a smooth stone and a sharp-edged stone and ask learners which one would be more useful for cutting meat, and why. Explain that today's lesson looks at the actual tools Stone Age people made and used. State the lesson goal.

Explain that Stone Age people shaped stones, mainly by chipping/flaking, into tools for specific tasks; tools became sharper and more specialised from the Early to the Late Stone Age. Explain hunting tools: spears and, later, bows with arrow heads, used to kill animals such as buffalo and antelope. Explain cutting tools: hand axes and stone knives/flakes, used to cut meat, skin animals and cut plant material. Explain digging tools: digging sticks, sometimes stone-tipped, and scrapers, used to dig up roots and tubers and to prepare hides. Zambian link: such tools have been excavated at Mumbwa Caves, Kalambo Falls and Kabwe, showing Zambia has rich Stone Age tool evidence used by archaeologists to study our past. Group Activity: In groups, learners match pictures/descriptions of tools to their correct use (hunting/cutting/digging) on a worksheet drawn on manila paper, and present their answers.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. Name TWO tools Stone Age people used for hunting. 2. What was a digging stick used for? 3. Kabaso says "a hand axe and a spear were used for exactly the same purpose." Using what you have learnt, explain to Kabaso why this is incorrect. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: The National Museums Board has asked your school's History Club to help set up labels for a Stone Age tools exhibition at the Livingstone Museum. Task 1: Identify the THREE main uses of Stone Age tools covered in this lesson. (6 marks) Task 2: For each use (hunting, cutting, digging), name and describe a suitable Stone Age tool. (9 marks) Task 3: Explain why studying such tools helps historians understand how Stone Age people lived. (5 marks)
Assign: "Draw and label three Stone Age tools (one for hunting, one for cutting and one for digging), and write one sentence explaining the use of each."
Recap: "Stone Age tools were used mainly for hunting, cutting and digging, and became more advanced over time." Preview: "Next, we will contrast the Stone Age way of life with modern way of life."
Contrasting the Stone Age way of life with the modern way of life.
Specific Competence 1.4.1.1: Draw lessons from Stone Age way of life (Contrasting Stone Age way of life with modern way of life).

Ask learners to imagine spending one full day living exactly like a Stone Age person, with no phone, no shop and no built house. Ask: "What would be the hardest part?" Explain that today's lesson compares Stone Age life with life today. State the lesson goal.

Draw a large Venn diagram on the chalkboard labelled 'Stone Age Life' and 'Modern Life'. Similarities: guide learners to identify common features - both need food, shelter and clothing; both use tools; both live in groups/communities; both have some form of leadership. Differences - Stone Age: lived in caves/rock shelters, nomadic (moved often), used stone tools, obtained food by hunting/gathering, no formal schools or hospitals, no money. Differences - Modern: live in built houses, for example in Lusaka, Kitwe or rural villages with brick homes; settled/permanent; use metal/machine tools and technology; obtain food through farming/formal jobs and buying from markets/shops; have schools, hospitals and money/banks. Group Activity: In pairs, learners sort five given statements into the correct part of the Venn diagram, e.g. 'used stone tools', 'lives in a brick house in Kitwe', 'gathers wild fruits for food', 'goes to Levy Mwanawasa Hospital when sick', 'needs food and shelter'. Synthesis: Review answers as a class and correct any misclassifications.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. State TWO similarities between Stone Age life and modern life. 2. State TWO differences between Stone Age life and modern life. 3. Kondwani says "modern people no longer need tools like Stone Age people did." Using what you have learnt, explain why Kondwani's statement is incorrect. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: Your school in Chipata has organised a 'Then and Now' exhibition for Founder's Day, comparing Stone Age life with life in modern Zambia. Task 1: State TWO ways Stone Age people obtained shelter and food, and compare each with how people in Chipata obtain shelter and food today. (8 marks) Task 2: Explain TWO differences in technology/tools between the Stone Age and modern Zambia. (8 marks) Task 3: Suggest one lesson modern Zambians can learn from the way Stone Age people cooperated as a community. (4 marks)
Assign: "Draw your own Venn diagram at home comparing how your grandparents grew up and how you live today, with at least two similarities and two differences."

Recap: "Stone Age life and modern life share basic human needs, but differ greatly in tools, shelter, food sources and technology." Preview: "Next, we will locate Stone Age sites on the map of Zambia."
Locating Stone Age sites on the map of Zambia, e.g. Mumbwa Caves, Nachikufu Caves, Gwisho Hot Springs.
General Competence: Analytical Thinking
General Competence: Digital Literacy
Specific Competence 1.4.2.1: Assess importance of Stone Age sites in Zambia (Locating Stone Age sites on the map of Zambia).

Display or draw a blank outline map of Zambia and ask learners to name any historical or heritage site they already know, for example Victoria Falls. Explain that many places in Zambia hold evidence of Stone Age life, and today we will locate some of them. State the lesson goal.

Explain that archaeologists have discovered Stone Age tools, bones and rock art at several sites across Zambia, mainly in caves, rock shelters and near water sources. Introduce and locate key sites on the map: Mumbwa Caves (Central Province) - Early/Middle Stone Age tools; Nachikufu Caves (Mpika, Muchinga Province) - Late Stone Age tools and rock paintings; Gwisho Hot Springs (Kafue Flats, Southern Province) - Late Stone Age site with well-preserved remains near hot springs; Kalambo Falls (Mbala, Northern Province) - one of the oldest and most important Early Stone Age sites in Africa; Mwela Rocks (near Kasama, Northern Province) - rock art site. For each site, briefly state what was found there and why it matters. Group Activity: In groups, learners use an outline map of Zambia drawn on manila paper to mark and label at least four Stone Age sites, referring to an atlas or wall map for correct province locations. Presentations: Groups present their labelled maps to the class. Synthesis: Complete a class map on the chalkboard showing all sites discussed.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. Name TWO Stone Age sites found in Zambia. 2. In which province is Kalambo Falls located? 3. Temba, a Form 1 pupil from Solwezi, believes Stone Age sites are "only found outside Zambia." Using what you have learnt, correct Temba with TWO examples. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: The Ministry of Tourism has invited your school's Geography-History Club to help produce a simple tourist map brochure showing Stone Age heritage sites in Zambia for visitors attending a conference in Lusaka. Task 1: Name and locate (by province) FOUR Stone Age sites in Zambia that should appear on the brochure map. (12 marks) Task 2: For any ONE of the sites named, briefly state what was discovered there. (4 marks) Task 3: Suggest one reason why accurately locating such sites on a map is useful for visitors and researchers. (4 marks)
Assign: "Using an atlas or map of Zambia, draw the outline of your own Province and mark any historical, cultural or Stone Age site you know of in it, or the nearest one to you."

Recap: "Zambia has several important Stone Age sites, including Mumbwa Caves, Nachikufu Caves, Gwisho Hot Springs, Kalambo Falls and Mwela Rocks." Preview: "Next, we will assess the importance of these Stone Age sites, focusing on tourism and cultural heritage."
Analysing the importance of Stone Age sites in Zambia, focusing on tourism and cultural heritage, and how to conserve them.
General Competence: Entrepreneurship
General Competence: Environmental Sustainability
Specific Competence 1.4.2.1: Assess importance of Stone Age sites in Zambia (Analysing the importance of Stone Age sites: Tourism, Cultural Heritage).

Narrate: "Every year, hundreds of tourists visit Kalambo Falls and nearby caves in Mbala to see evidence of the earliest humans in the region." Ask: "Why do you think people travel from far to see old stones and caves?" State the lesson goal: "Today we explain the importance of Stone Age sites in Zambia."

Explain tourism importance: Stone Age sites attract local and international tourists and researchers, creating income for local communities (through guiding, crafts, accommodation and food) and for government (through entry fees and taxes), and creating jobs such as tour guides, curators and vendors. Explain cultural heritage importance: these sites preserve evidence of Zambia's earliest history and identity, connecting present-day Zambians to their ancient past and promoting national pride, similar to how Victoria Falls and traditional ceremonies are preserved and celebrated. Explain educational/research importance: sites provide real evidence for historians, archaeologists and learners to study human origins and technological development, supporting education and scientific research both locally and internationally. Explain conservation: because these sites are fragile and non-renewable - once destroyed they cannot be replaced - it is important to protect them from vandalism, indiscriminate mining/quarrying, littering and uncontrolled development, by sensitising communities and involving traditional leaders and heritage clubs. Group Activity: In groups, learners design a simple poster/slogan encouraging Zambians to visit and protect a named Stone Age site, e.g. 'Visit Kalambo Falls - Protect Our Ancient Story', and identify one business opportunity linked to the site. Synthesis: Complete Fig 1.4g on the chalkboard showing Tourism, Cultural Heritage, Education/Research and National recognition.

Instruct individual work. Questions: 1. State TWO ways Stone Age sites benefit Zambia through tourism. 2. Why are Stone Age sites important as cultural heritage? 3. Mwaba complains that "old caves and stones with no gold are useless and should be dug up for other uses." Using what you have learnt about the importance of Stone Age sites, explain to Mwaba TWO reasons why he is wrong. 4. ECSEOL-STYLE SCENARIO QUESTION: You are a member of the Junior Council at your school near Nachikufu Caves in Mpika. The District Tourism Office has invited your council to advise on how to promote and protect the caves for both tourism and future generations. Task 1: Explain TWO ways Nachikufu Caves, or a similar Stone Age site, could generate income for the local community through tourism. (8 marks) Task 2: Explain TWO reasons why such a site is important as part of Zambia's cultural heritage. (6 marks) Task 3: Suggest TWO measures the community/council could take to protect the site from destruction. (6 marks)
Assign: "Write a half-page proposal titled 'How My Community Can Benefit From and Protect a Nearby Heritage Site', using at least three points learnt in this topic."

Recap: "Stone Age sites in Zambia are important for tourism, cultural heritage and education, and must be protected for future generations." Preview: "Next, we will begin Topic 1.5: The Beginning and Spread of Iron Working and Farming."

obc_2013__re2046__g10__10_1_birth_and_in.topicName: 10.1 Birth and Infancy of John the Baptist and Jesus
notes: Exploring and appreciating traditional Zambian postnatal practices and naming ceremonies.
Describe what happens after a baby has been born in their families.
Explain how names are chosen and given to infants in their families.
Asks what a family does first when a newborn arrives home, then introduces the lesson as an exploration of Zambian birth traditions and the values they carry (community, identity).

Defines birth traditions and discusses common Zambian postnatal practices — the Chilanga Mulilo kitchen-fire ceremony, seclusion of mother and baby, relatives' gift-bearing visits — and naming practices (honouring grandparents, circumstances of birth, religious meaning). Sets a group task: list 3 postnatal practices and the value each teaches.

Poses individual questions on traditional practices after a birth, naming a child after a grandparent, how Chilanga Mulilo shows community, and responding to the claim that such ceremonies are 'old-fashioned'.
Assigns an interview task: ask a parent or grandparent the story behind the learner's own name, or what traditional practice marked their own birth.
Recaps that Zambian birth traditions are about community support, blessing, and identity, then links forward to how another culture (biblical) marked a very important birth: John the Baptist.

obc_2013__re2046__g10__10_1_birth_and_in.topicName: 10.1 Birth and Infancy of John the Baptist and Jesus
notes: Analyzing the biblical narrative of John the Baptist's birth and its prophetic significance.
Relate from Luke's Gospel the stories of the announcement of the birth of John and his naming.
Explain John the Baptist's life and Ministry.
Narrate how the life and Ministry of John the Baptist were a fulfilment of the Old Testament prophecy.
Recalls how Zambian families announce a birth, then hooks with the story of an elderly couple visited by an angel with unbelievable news.

Narrates Luke 1:5-25 (the angel Gabriel's announcement to Zechariah) and 1:57-66 (John's birth and naming), highlighting Zechariah's doubt and temporary muteness and the naming dispute; defines 'prophet' and 'forerunner'; connects John's wilderness ministry to the Isaiah 40:3 and Malachi 3:1 prophecies.
Poses questions on why Zechariah lost his speech, why John's naming defied family custom, and how his adult ministry fulfilled Isaiah 40:3.
Assigns a 4-panel comic strip depicting the angel's appearance, John's birth, the naming argument, and Zechariah regaining speech.
Recaps that John's birth and life were mapped out by prophecy as the Messiah's forerunner, then links to an even greater birth announcement to come: Jesus.

obc_2013__re2046__g10__10_1_birth_and_in.topicName: 10.1 Birth and Infancy of John the Baptist and Jesus
notes: Analyzing the nativity story in Luke and Matthew, focusing on divine announcements and prophetic fulfilment.
Describe the announcement of the birth of Jesus to various people.
Describe the birth of Jesus Christ.
Explain how these stories were a fulfilment of the Old Testament prophecies.
Uses a familiar Christmas carol to link to Jesus's birth, then focuses learners on the actual biblical accounts and the prophecies behind them.

Guides comparative reading of Luke's account (to Mary, to shepherds) and Matthew's (to Joseph in a dream, to the Magi), fills a comparison chart, reads Luke 2:1-7 highlighting the humble setting, and introduces Isaiah 7:14 and Micah 5:2 as fulfilled prophecies.
Poses questions comparing Mary's and Joseph's responses, the angel's reassurance to the shepherds, and the significance of Bethlehem per Micah 5:2.
Assigns a poster on 'The First Christmas Announcements', listing the four announcements (to Mary, Joseph, shepherds, Magi).
Recaps that Jesus's birth was announced to humble and wise alike and fulfilled precise prophecies, then links forward to a childhood incident that caused his parents worry.

obc_2013__re2046__g10__10_1_birth_and_in.topicName: 10.1 Birth and Infancy of John the Baptist and Jesus
notes: Identifying and analyzing common causes of conflict in parent-child relationships.
Identify sources of misunderstanding and conflict between parents and children.
Asks learners to acknowledge disagreements with a parent/guardian, framing conflict as normal and the lesson as about understanding its causes.

Defines conflict and elicits sources — generation gap, communication breakdown, unmet expectations, social/economic stress, media influence, the struggle for independence — then discusses Zambian-specific factors (respect for elders/Chishimba, lobola discussions, pressure to contribute to family income). Runs a role-play analysis in groups using scenario slips.
Poses questions on a hairstyle disagreement, how poor communication escalates conflict, and the positive intention behind a parent's traditional statement.
Assigns a reflection on a real or recalled conflict moment at home: the surface argument versus the deeper underlying concern.
Recaps that conflict often stems from generation gaps, communication issues, unmet expectations, and stress, then links to a childhood incident that caused Jesus's own parents worry.

obc_2013__re2046__g10__10_1_birth_and_in.topicName: 10.1 Birth and Infancy of John the Baptist and Jesus
notes: Examining the presentation of baby Jesus at the Temple and the episode of the 12-year-old Jesus in the Temple.
Relate from Luke's gospel the stories about Jesus in the Temple as a baby and at 12 years.
Recalls the previous lesson on parent-child misunderstandings, then hooks with Jesus's Temple presentation as a baby, drawing a parallel to Zambian infant-dedication customs.

Narrates Luke 2:22-40 (the presentation, Simeon's prophecy that Jesus would be a light for the nations and a sword would pierce Mary's soul, and Anna's recognition of him) and Luke 2:41-52 (the 12-year-old Jesus staying behind at the Temple, found after 3 days questioning the teachers, and his reply 'Didn't you know I had to be in my Father's house?'). Leads discussion on how Jesus balanced obedience to his earthly parents with his sense of a higher duty.

Poses questions on what Simeon and Anna's presence reveals about God's plans spanning generations, the source of the Temple conflict (linking back to Lesson 10.1.4's term), and what Jesus's statement reveals about his own identity.
Assigns a diary entry from Mary's perspective on the night they found the 12-year-old Jesus in the Temple, describing her worry, relief, and confusion.
Recaps that Jesus's childhood showed unique devotion to God alongside obedience to his earthly parents, then links to how the Bible teaches God directs human lives.

obc_2013__re2046__g10__10_1_birth_and_in.topicName: 10.1 Birth and Infancy of John the Baptist and Jesus
notes: Synthesizing lessons from the infancy narratives about God's methods of guidance.
Explain what the infancy narratives in the Gospel of Luke and Matthew teach about God's direction of human lives.
Uses a maze/winding-road image to ask who or what guides people's lives, then focuses learners on identifying HOW God directed events in the stories already studied.

Reviews the major events, then guides learners to identify God's five methods of direction: through angels/messengers, through dreams, through prophecy and scripture, through circumstances (the census, the star), and through people (Elizabeth, Simeon, Anna). Defines 'Divine Providence'.

Poses questions on God's use of a Roman census, the contrast between how God guided Zechariah versus the Magi, and the connection between hearing and obeying God's direction (Mary's 'may your word be fulfilled').
Assigns a reflection on a real decision the learner is making, explaining how one of the five methods could apply today.
Recaps the five methods of divine direction, then links to how Christians today can identify and respond to God's direction.

obc_2013__re2046__g10__10_1_birth_and_in.topicName: 10.1 Birth and Infancy of John the Baptist and Jesus
obc_2013__re2046__g10__10_1_birth_and_in.subTopicName: How Christians Can Identify and Respond to God's Direction
notes: Translating biblical principles of divine guidance into practical steps for contemporary Christian living.
Discuss how Christians today can identify and respond to God's direction of their lives.
Asks whether learners have wished for a clear sign like Joseph's dream when facing a big decision, then focuses on practical everyday ways Christians can identify God's direction.

Teaches the 'Five Lamps' framework for discernment using Psalm 119:105: the Lamp of Scripture, the Lamp of Prayer, the Lamp of Wise Counsel, the Lamp of Circumstances, and the Lamp of Peace — then how to respond, with obedience, trust, and patience.

Poses questions on why the Lamp of Scripture is the most important check, what questions to ask a friend who feels led to drop out of school for music, and when patient waiting is the correct response.
Assigns a week-long 'Guidance Journal': noting one decision each day and which Lamp was or could have been used.
Recaps the Five Lamps and the required response of obedience, trust and patience, then links to how other major religions in Zambia understand God's direction.

obc_2013__re2046__g10__10_1_birth_and_in.topicName: 10.1 Birth and Infancy of John the Baptist and Jesus
obc_2013__re2046__g10__10_1_birth_and_in.subTopicName: Christian, Muslim and Hindu Teachings on How God Directs Human Lives
notes: Comparing and contrasting the concepts of divine guidance in Christianity, Islam, and Hinduism.
Compare Christian, Muslim and Hindu teaching on how God directs human lives.

Asks where Zambians facing a big problem might seek guidance (pastor/Bible, Imam/Quran, Hindu priest/holy books, sangoma/ancestral spirits), then frames the lesson as a respectful comparison of three major world religions.

Reviews the Christian view (Bible, Holy Spirit, prayer, counsel, circumstances, a personal relationship through Jesus), explains the Islamic view (Tawhid — the Quran as Allah's literal final word, the Hadith, submission to Sharia), and the Hindu view (Vedas/Upanishads/Bhagavad Gita, the concept of Dharma, gurus, life-cycle rites/Samskaras), then facilitates comparison of similarities and differences.

Poses questions on how Christians and Muslims differ in viewing their holy books, the role of a Hindu guru versus a similar Christian figure, and what career-guidance source each religion's follower would consult.
Assigns an interview of a Muslim or Hindu classmate/family member/neighbour (or research) on how their faith guides their decisions.
Recaps that Christians rely on the Bible and Holy Spirit, Muslims on the Quran and Sharia, and Hindus on Dharma and gurus, closing Topic 10.1 and transitioning to John the Baptist's adult ministry.

obc_2013__re2046__g10__10_2_ministry_and.topicName: 10.2 Ministry and Death of John the Baptist
notes: Identifying contemporary Zambian voices and organizations that challenge social and moral wrongs.
Identify organisations and people in Zambia who denounce sin and evil in the nation.
Writes 'SPEAK TRUTH TO POWER' on the board and asks who does this, then links John's confrontation of Herod to modern 'John the Baptists' in Zambia.

Defines 'denounce' and outlines categories of modern voices — religious leaders, civil society organizations (e.g. Transparency International Zambia), activists/journalists, and artists/musicians — with brief real Zambian case studies (a church body speaking against gender-based violence, an NGO reporting misuse of school funds, a musician's song on alcoholism).
Poses questions on why religious leaders should address social issues, naming a Zambian organization and its method, and how to respectfully speak against lunch-money theft at school.
Assigns a short respectful 'public statement' denouncing a local community issue and proposing a positive change.
Recaps that speaking against evil is the role of religious leaders, CSOs, activists, and responsible citizens alike, then links to John's specific preached message.

obc_2013__re2046__g10__10_2_ministry_and.topicName: 10.2 Ministry and Death of John the Baptist
obc_2013__re2046__g10__10_2_ministry_and.subTopicName: The Message of John the Baptist
notes: Analyzing the core themes of John's preaching: Repentance, Change of Behaviour, and Baptism.
Outline the main message of John the Baptist.
Shows the 'REPENT!' sign and asks how learners would react to seeing it held by a man in camel hair, then frames the lesson as breaking down John's urgent message.

Guides reading of Luke 3:1-14 and outlines the three-fold message: Repentance (metanoia — a decisive change of mind and direction), Change of Behaviour/Fruit (John's practical examples: sharing, honesty, not extorting), and Baptism (a public sign of repentance and cleansing, Mark 1:4), motivated by the nearness of God's kingdom.
Poses questions distinguishing feeling sorry from true repentance, which modern profession might receive John's tax-collector advice, and why baptism mattered.
Assigns a modern-day rewrite of Luke 3:7-14's speech, addressing a similar group in Zambian society today.
Recaps the three-fold message (repent, change actions, be baptized) as preparation for Jesus, then links to applying it in Zambia today.

obc_2013__re2046__g10__10_2_ministry_and.topicName: 10.2 Ministry and Death of John the Baptist
notes: Translating John the Baptist's ethical teachings into specific, positive actions for contemporary Zambian society.
Explain how John the Baptist's instructions about right behaviour could be applied in Zambia today.
Recalls John's specific commands and asks what he'd address if he spoke at a school assembly today, framing the lesson as crafting modern instructions for right behaviour.

Reviews John's core principles (generosity, honesty, fairness/non-violence, integrity) and their application across school, home, community/market, and national levels, then sets a group 'Code of Conduct' poster task per sector.
Poses questions on a marketeer selling underweight goods, a bus conductor tempted to overcharge, sharing in the classroom, and a PSA against exam malpractice.
Assigns practicing one of John's principles for a day and writing a diary entry about the experience.
Recaps that John's message calls for generosity, honesty, and fairness in every area of life, then links to comparing John's work with Jesus's.

obc_2013__re2046__g10__10_2_ministry_and.topicName: 10.2 Ministry and Death of John the Baptist
obc_2013__re2046__g10__10_2_ministry_and.subTopicName: The Work of John and That of Jesus
notes: Contrasting and connecting the ministries of John (the forerunner) and Jesus (the Messiah).
Compare the work of John with that of Jesus.
Uses a road-grader/motorcade analogy — John preparing the road, Jesus the king arriving — to frame comparing their work.

Guides reading of Matthew 3:11-12, John 1:29-34, and Matthew 11:7-11, filling a T-chart contrasting John's work (preached repentance, baptized with water, called for moral reform, could not forgive sins) with Jesus's (preached the Kingdom, forgave sins, healed, baptized with the Holy Spirit, died and rose), highlighting that John dealt with sinful behaviour while Jesus dealt with sin itself, though both called people to turn to God.
Poses questions on the symbolic difference between water and Holy Spirit baptism, why only Jesus could forgive sins, and correcting the claim that John and Jesus were 'basically the same'.
Assigns a dialogue between John and Jesus meeting at the Jordan, with Jesus explaining how his work continues and completes John's.
Recaps John as preparation and Jesus as fulfilment, then links to how people responded to John's challenging message.

obc_2013__re2046__g10__10_2_ministry_and.topicName: 10.2 Ministry and Death of John the Baptist
obc_2013__re2046__g10__10_2_ministry_and.subTopicName: Responses to Religious and Moral Messages in Zambia
notes: Analyzing the spectrum of public reactions to prophetic or moral voices in contemporary Zambia.
